substrate layer 5 mm into the sphere. This also has the important advantage that

measurement is done for powder layers on real AM-built substrates thus mimicking

real build conditions. It is also critical that the calibration target and samples used

for measurement are placed in the same position, so calibration targets for this work5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             115



were cut to roughly match the substrate size so they ﬁt inside the sample port.

   Previous implementations of ISR in laser-based manufacturing experiments have

predominantly been carried out at normal incidence, and therefore included an ad-

ditional photodiode intended to measure back-reﬂections of the laser beam through

the top of the sphere (which commonly occurred at the start of laser-melting exper-

iments) [25]. Adding this additional photodiode would have been impossible in this

commercial additive system. This is one of the original reasons behind the decision

to process at 11°, as described above.  In this experiment, the presence of powder

should limit specular reﬂection from the sample in general, and if they occur, direct

reﬂections should tend toward the opposite sphere wall. This did come with concerns

about burning the interior coating with high-power specular reﬂections, but inspec-

tion of the sphere during and after the experiments revealed no visible damage, and

there was no systematic degradation in sphere signal observed over the course of the

experiment.

   The output port includes a 2 mm hole with half of a FC/PC ﬁbre port mounted on

the outside. A multi-mode ﬁbre with a 200 µm core and numerical aperture (NA) of

0.22 (Thorlabs M122L05) is connected to this ﬁbre port, delivering the tip of the ﬁbre

ﬂush with the interior sphere wall. The NA of the ﬁbre informed the design of the

baﬄe, ensuring only light that has reﬂected multiple times can enter the ﬁbre. The

ﬁbre passes through an airtight port on a custom cap for an unused powder exhaust

port on the Renishaw AM 400.  Light from the ﬁbre enters free space through a

terminated ﬁbre adapter (Thorlabs SM1FC) and passes through an assembly of ﬁlters

before reaching the detector. The ﬁrst is an ND 0.5 ﬁlter (measured as 0.500 ± 0.001)

that compensates for the lower powers used in the calibration process (explained in5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             116



Sec. 5.3.3). The second is a 1070 nm laser line band-pass ﬁlter that ensures only light

from the processing laser is measured by the photodiode (e.g., eliminating blackbody

radiation). Any blackbody radiation near the processing laser wavelength is estimated

to be orders of magnitude lower in power compared to the scattered laser light, and

so is considered negligible. The optical path from the ﬁbre adapter to the detector

is stable as all the components are held together by threaded mounts and screwed

onto the photodiode directly. For the ﬁxed distance from ﬁbre tip to detector, the

max spot size of the beam from the ﬁbre ﬁlls most of the detector area. When the

ND ﬁlter is removed during calibration, an empty optical mount of the same size is

put in its place to maintain this constant distance. The rise time of the photodiode

(Thorlabs PDA100A2) at the gain setting used in this work (30 dB) is 3.8 µs. The

output of the photodiode is recorded by an oscilloscope (Tektronix DPO-3034) at a

time resolution of 1 µs. Data acquisition is handled by a custom LabVIEW program.


Measuring the input power


ISR measurements require accurate and speciﬁc knowledge of input laser power as a

function of time. This is typically gained through separate measurements of laser en-

ergy and pulse shape for every individual parameter set planned for the experiment.

Photodiodes can provide time-resolved intensity proﬁles, but since incident powers

must be limited to avoid damage, they are not usually compatible with absolute

measurements for the powers required in AM. Power/energy meters can withstand

such high powers, but typically do not give high temporal resolution. Combining the

two allows time-resolved calibrated measurement. In its most straightforward imple-

mentation, the laser would be controlled to generate a top hat of speciﬁc duration5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             117



and resolved by the photodiode. Since the integral of this trace is pulse energy, the

absolute scale can be calibrated using an energy meter to capture the pulse energy.

  We ﬁnd that to achieve similar results in commercial AM systems is more compli-

cated, particularly in single point exposure systems like the Renishaw AM 400 used

in this study. Typical AM control software was not intended for this sort of measure-

ment so does not allow the detailed control described above. In addition, the system

generates a more complicated intensity waveform than just a square wave; that is,

pulse intensity decreases between pulses but does not reach zero. The eﬀective mod-

ulation frequency of this laser output exceeded the speciﬁed maximum frequency of

the available power meter, so it was not possible to directly measure total energy

contained in a typical pulse train.

  A three-step measurement system was devised to overcome these challenges: (1)

measure calibrated power for the long pulse emission, (2) capture the uncalibrated

intensity trace for each parameter set used for the multi-track experiments, and (3)

capture uncalibrated intensity traces of both short and long pulses together from

the same power set point. From (3), the peak intensity of the short pulses can be

compared to the top hat intensity of the long pulses. Then from (1) and (2), the

calibrated average power from the long pulse can be scaled appropriately to the peak

power of the short pulses, thereby producing a calibrated pulse train of power as a

function of time.

   Average laser power was measured for 1 s to 2 s long pulses using a commercial

power meter (PRIMES Cube, Germany). The meter was mounted in the center of

the build plate (location marked using the laser) and the build plate was lowered to

−300 mm to achieve the speciﬁed minimum spot size on the absorbing surface of the5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             118



power meter of 5 mm (conﬁrmed using photosensitive paper). The Renishaw AM 400

was operated at an access level that allowed manual ﬁring of the laser at any power

setting with minimum duration of 1 s. This mode is only used for calibration and

servicing of the machine and is not used at any future point in the experiment. The

power meter also has an energy threshold of 50 J for accurate measurement, so some

of the lower power settings needed 2 s exposures.

   Pulse train shapes for the experiment were captured next. Ideally, the laser would

be kept stationary, defocused signiﬁcantly, and incident on a diﬀuse target. Then,

a photodiode placed nearby could passively measure time-resolved laser output with

no other variables aﬀecting signal level.  However, due to constraints of the AM

machine interface, it was unfeasible to program the laser to ﬁre a stationary pulse

train to match relevant pulse trains for the experiment. A workaround was developed

where the machine was programmed to “build” tracks that matched all the same

parameters to be used in the multi-track experiments (length, exposure time, point

distance, hatch spacing, etc.) except it was positioned in the center of the build plate.

The scanning beam would eﬀect the signal measured at a stationary photodiode, so

there was a now a need to eliminate, or at least mitigate, this positional dependence.

A diﬀuse gold target (later used for calibration) was placed in the path of the laser

beam, and the bottom half of the integrating sphere was placed upside-down on top

of the target, with the ﬁbre installed. The build plate was again lowered to −300 mm

to defocus the beam. The result is a ﬁbre-coupled free-space reﬂective diﬀuser. The

long dimension of the bottom sphere opening is aligned in the direction of the laser

scan pattern. Even 300 mm below the focal plane, the laser beam scans through the

opening of the sphere and hits the gold target, scattering diﬀusely inside the half5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             119



sphere and coupling into the ﬁbre to be detected. This did not completely remove

the spatial dependence on the signal, as the signal did drop slightly in the middle of

the scan path, but since this was highly reproducible it could be normalized after the

fact. After normalizing to achieve relative uniformity in peak height, the measured

signal still needs to be related to the measured power, and this is achieved by the

next measurement.

    Lastly, the two previous measurements are linked by

next measurement.

short pulses to average signal in long pulse operation. To be clear, the goal is to

relate the uncalibrated, normalized laser output traces captured in step 2 to the

calibrated laser output power measured in step 1. The physical set up is the same as

the pulse train measurements above. Signal level from 5 pulses each of 30 µs, 60 µs,

80 µs, 100 µs, and most of a single 1 s pulse at the same set point power were captured

in the same measurement window. Importantly, the pulses are all aimed very close

to the center of the target (within 30 µm), so there is no spatial dependence in the

signal. There was a clear and consistent ratio between the peak signal of the short

pulses and the mean steady-state signal from the long pulse. In this case, the peak

signal from the short pulses was taken as the mean of the 10 highest points within

the range of 20 points centered on the peak value. The ratio of peak signal level to

steady-state signal level for the same power is 99.98 % for 100 µs pulses, 99.67 % for

80 µs pulses, 98.9 % for 60 µs pulses, and 92.7 % for 30 µs pulses. These ratios were

used to convert the raw signal of the pulse trains measured in step 2 to calculated

input power as a function of time.5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             120



Measuring the reﬂected power inside the integrating sphere


Measurements of reﬂected power during AM experiments are made possible by cal-

ibrating the integrating sphere. This was achieved by measuring sphere photodiode

signal while hitting a diﬀuse sample of known reﬂectance with pulses of known laser

power. A diﬀuse reﬂective calibration target (Infragold, Labsphere, USA), with re-

ﬂectance at 1070 nm of 93 %, was placed in one of the planned substrate positions

before printing. The calibration sample was cut to match the size of the substrates,

so it ﬁlled the entire sample port and sat at the same height inside the sphere. With

the sphere installed on the target, a series of 9 pulses was ﬁred at 75 locations (675

total pulses) arranged in a grid pattern that sparsely covered the full extent of the

target surface. By sampling many positions on the calibration target, the combined

uncertainty due to variations of the target reﬂectivity and spatial non-uniformity of

the sphere were incorporated into the calibration. The signals generated by these

pulses were measured over a range of 8 powers from 45 W–65 W. This procedure was

repeated for each substrate position, but due to an error in the procedure one of the

attempts is discarded. The slopes of the resulting linear relationships for incident

power versus photodiode signal were slightly diﬀerent for each position, so all data

were combined together so that the variance from diﬀerent calibrations would factor

into the uncertainty in the ﬁnal linear ﬁt (Fig. 5.2). This ﬁt gave a slope representing

power as a function of photodiode signal, called the calibration factor, C = 569 W/V.

   One challenge in calibrating an integrating sphere for laser-based manufacturing

experiments is avoiding damage to the calibration target while still achieving compa-

rable signal levels expected for the real experiment. The main method to solve this

involves lowering laser power as much as necessary to avoid damage to the calibration5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             121





Figure 5.2: Calibration data used to determine relationship between measured signal
and reﬂected power. The calibration is performed with input power as the indepen-
dent variable, but the important output is the slope of power as a function of signal.
Each circle represents the average signal measured from 75 diﬀerent locations on the
target. The diﬀerent colours denote the three series of measurements from diﬀerent
substrate locations. The black dashed line represents the ﬁt from the linear regres-
sion (including all data points). It is extended to zero to show that the ﬁt is forced
through the origin.

experiment, adds some uncertainty due to the ND value of the ﬁlter, but overall low-

In this work, the small spot size of the laser posed a further challenge, so in addition

a 207 µm spot size. It was conﬁrmed experimentally that changing the spot size did

                             PA(t) = P0(t) −PR(t).                            (5.1)

by the average signal of a long, square pulse at the same power (Section 5.3.3). This

varied by pulse duration, but showed no trend with set point power, so an average

value was taken for each pulse duration. The M values and uncertainty are listed in

Table 5.1. The uncertainty reported in Table 5.1 corresponds to standard deviation

5.4  Results and Discussion


ISR absorptance measurements were performed for a total of 144 unique parameter

sets; varying laser power, laser beam spot size, exposure time, and most importantly,

sample surface condition. The results presented in this work will include a subset

of the total collection of time-resolved absorptance data as well as comprehensive

time-averaged data, mainly showcasing the stark diﬀerences between sample surface

conditions. For convenience, the four sample surface conditions will be given short-

powder (AM0), AM-printed substrate with 30 µm nominal powder thickness (AM30),

and AM-printed substrate with 90 µm nominal powder thickness (AM90). It is also

worth noting at this point that due to powder loss, the nominal powder thicknesses

are based on build stage drop distance, but the actual thickness of the powder layer

left on top of the substrates is likely at least 4 times higher than that [42, 59–63].5.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                             126

two should theoretically re-coat directly onto that. So the AM90 thickness can be

considered as AM30 plus 60 µm, likely somewhere above 180 µm. The exact values

are unknown, but most importantly, this matches the true conditions in a AM build.

Throughout this section, distinction between conduction mode, transition mode, and

keyhole mode are made by observation of the data sets involving no powder, since in

these cases the presence of keyhole-enhanced absorptance increase is easy to distin-

guish against the high reﬂectivity of bare aluminum (this will be explained in more

detail later).

Abstract:
The use of components fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) requires the development of processing parameters that can produce high-quality material. Manipulating the most commonly identified critical build parameters (e.g., laser power, laser scan speed, and layer thickness) on LPBF equipment can generate acceptable parts for established materials and moderately intricate part geometries. The need to fabricate increasingly complex parts from unique materials drives the limited research into LPBF process control using underutilized parameters, such as atmosphere composition and pressure. As presented in this review, manipulating atmosphere composition and pressure in laser beam welding has been shown to expand processing windows and produce higher-quality welds. The similarities between laser beam welding and laser-based AM processes suggest that this atmosphere control research could be effectively adapted for LPBF, an area that has not been widely explored. Tailoring this research for LPBF has significant potential to reveal novel processing regimes. This review presents the current state of the art in atmosphere research for laser beam welding and LPBF, with a focus on studies exploring cover gas composition and pressure, and concludes with an outlook on future LPBF atmosphere control systems.

Abstract:
Keyhole porosity is a key concern in laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF), potentially impacting component fatigue life. However, some keyhole porosity formation mechanisms, e.g., keyhole fluctuation, collapse and bubble growth and shrinkage, remain unclear. Using synchrotron X-ray imaging we reveal keyhole and bubble behaviour, quantifying their formation dynamics. The findings support the hypotheses that: (i) keyhole porosity can initiate not only in unstable, but also in the transition keyhole regimes created by high laser power-velocity conditions, causing fast radial keyhole fluctuations (2.5–10 kHz); (ii) transition regime collapse tends to occur part way up the rear-wall; and (iii) immediately after keyhole collapse, bubbles undergo rapid growth due to pressure equilibration, then shrink due to metal-vapour condensation. Concurrent with condensation, hydrogen diffusion into the bubble slows the shrinkage and stabilises the bubble size. The keyhole fluctuation and bubble evolution mechanisms revealed here may guide the development of control systems for minimising porosity. Understanding the keyhole porosity formation is important in laser powder bed fusion. Here the authors reveal the dynamics of keyhole fluctuation, and collapse that induces bubble formation with three main stages of evolution; growth, shrinkage, and being captured by the solidification front.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific

Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

quotes, additional tags, etc.).

so that the artifact is properly contextualized.

Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. Question: what laser absorptance has been MEASURED (integrating sphere or calorimetry) at 1.03-1.08 um for aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, Al 6061, Al 5182, Al 1100, pure Al) under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode and in the transition just before a keyhole forms, on bare plates and on powder layers? Include Simonds et al. 2024 (AM-Bench 2022, Al 5182), Trapp et al. 2017, Matthews et al. 2018 (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302), and any AlSi10Mg single-track absorptance. Give the power, speed, spot size, the measured absorptance against time or power, and the DOI with the figure or table number. Is the higher value attributed to surface oxide, ripples, a shallow depression, or vapour?

Relevant Snippet:
The effective absorptivity of continuous wave 1070 nm laser light has been studied for bare and metal powder-coated discs of 316L stainless steel as well as for aluminum alloy 1100 and tungsten by use of direct calorimetric measurements. After carefully validating the applicability of the method, the effective absorptivity is plotted as a function of incident laser power from 30 up to ≈540 W for scanning speeds of 100, 500 and 1500 mm s−1. The effective absorptivity versus power curves of the bulk materials typically show a slight change in effective absorptivity from 30 W until the onset of the formation of a recoil pressure-induced surface depression. As observed using high-speed video, this change in surface morphology leads to an increase in absorption of the laser light. At the higher powers beyond the keyhole transition, a saturation value is reached for both bare discs and powder-coated disks. For ≈100 μm thick powder layers, the measured absorptivity was found to be two times that of the bare polished discs for low-laser power. There is a sharp decrease when full melting of the powder tracks is achieved, followed by a keyhole-driven increase at higher powers, similar to the bare disc case. It is shown that, under conditions associated with laser powder-bed fusion additive manufacturing, absorptivity values can vary greatly, and differ from both powder-layer measurements and liquid metal estimates from the literature.

## 1. Ability to Simulate Absorption and Melt Pool Dynamics for Laser Melting of Bare Aluminum Plate: Results and Insights from the 2022 Asynchronous AM-Bench Challenge

    title = "Ability to Simulate Absorption and Melt Pool Dynamics for Laser Melting of Bare Aluminum Plate: Results and Insights from the 2022 Asynchronous AM-Bench Challenge",

Abstract:
The 2022 Asynchronous AM-Bench challenge was designed to test the ability of simulations to accurately predict laser power absorption as well as various melt pool behaviors (width, depth, and solidification) during laser melting of solid metal during stationary and scanned laser illumination. In this challenge, participants were asked to predict a series of experimental outcomes. Experimental data were obtained from a series of experiments performed at the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratories in 2019. These experiments combined integrating sphere radiometry with high-speed X-ray imaging, allowing for the simultaneous recording of absolute laser power absorption and two-dimensional, projected images of the melt pool. All challenge problems were based on experiments using bare aluminum solid metal. Participants were provided with pertinent experimental information like laser power, scan speed, laser spot size, and material composition. Additionally, participants were given absorptance and X-ray imaging data from stationary and scanned laser experiments on solid Ti–6Al–4V that could be used for testing their models before attempting challenge problems. In total, this challenge received 56 submissions from eight different research groups for eight individual challenge problems. The data for this challenge, and associated information, are available for download from the NIST Public Data Repository. This paper summarizes the results from the 2022 Asynchronous AM-Bench challenge as well as discusses the lessons learned to help inform future challenges.

Abstract:
Laser melting can be conducted in two different process regimes, the conduction and the keyhole mode, which exhibit significantly different characteristics, dynamics, and stability and are highly sensitive to a magnitude of process parameters. Despite these differences and the resulting high relevance of the prevailing process regime for process development, the regime is commonly deduced after specimen testing. An identification of the regime parallel to the process could speed up the process development of, for example, laser beam welding or laser-based powder bed fusion of metals. Therefore, the possibility of an in situ regime identification under process-near conditions is the aim of these investigations. For this, the absorbance is measured in situ by using an integrating sphere on an in-house-developed test rig. This test rig can mimic real production process conditions to detect the characteristic change in the degree of absorption when switching between the process regimes. These measurements were conducted during experiments in which only the laser power was varied. A significant change in absorption was detected at a threshold laser power of 100 W, which correlates with the transition between the process regimes’ conduction and keyhole regime. This threshold was proven by subsequent identification analysis of micrographic cross sections. This correlation promises the possibility of fast in situ process regime identification under near-real production process conditions with the potential of accelerating process development.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of SiCp/AlSi10Mg is promising in many industrial fields. In this paper, the characteristics of a 15 wt.% 1200 mesh SiCp/AlSi10Mg metal matrix composite fabricated by LPBF were investigated systematically, i.e., from a single track to a block. It was found that when the laser energy input was high enough, the single track was continuous and not distorted; when the laser energy input was low, the single track was unstable and wrinkled. The densification of the LPBFed composite sample was influenced significantly by the surface morphologies and geometric dimensions of the single tracks. As high as 98.9% relative density was achieved when the optimized processing parameters were used. Because of the good wettability and the interfacial reaction during the process, the interface of SiC and the matrix showed good bonding. Near the interface of SiC and the matrix, needle-shaped phase Al4SiC4 could be found both in the single track and block, and the faceted particle Si was formed in the block because of the interfacial reaction. The microhardness of the LPBFed SiCp/AlSi10Mg composites was much higher than that of the LPBFed unreinforced AlSi10Mg. A coefficient of friction of 0.178 and wear rate of 2.02 × 10−4 mm3/(N⋅m) were achieved for the LPBFed composites. The main wear mechanism was delamination wear, accompanied by abrasive wear. The maximum yield strength and ultimate compressive strength were 566.6 MPa and 764.1 MPa, respectively. The fracture mode of the LPBFed composites is mainly brittle fracture. This study provides a theoretical and technical basis for LPBFed SiCp/AlSi10Mg 3D parts.

Abstract:
The quantification of absorbed light is essential for understanding laser-material interactions and melt pool dynamics in order to minimize defects in additively manufactured metal components. The geometry of a vapor depression formed during laser melting is closely related to laser energy absorption. This relationship has been observed by the state-of-the-art in situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray visualization and integrating sphere radiometry. These two techniques create a temporally resolved dataset consisting of vapor depression images and corresponding laser absorptance. In this work, we propose two different approaches to predict instantaneous laser absorptance. The end-to-end approach uses deep convolutional neural networks to learn implicit features of X-ray images automatically and predict the laser energy absorptance. The two-stage approach uses a semantic segmentation model to engineer geometric features and predict absorptance using classical regression models. While having distinct advantages, both approaches achieved a consistently low mean absolute error of less than 3.3%.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Melt-pool depth governs interlayer bonding and porosity in laser powder bed fusion and underpins part qualification, yet predicting it reliably remains difficult. Fast conduction models reach useful accuracy only after the absorptivity is fitted to the depths they are meant to predict, and inverse analyses have been used the same way, to recover a calibrated parameter rather than to test the model. Here, the absorptivity is fixed independently instead, a measured coupling for IN718 and, for IN625 and 316L, a published closed-form relation never fitted to the present depths. This converts a moving-source conduction model from an object of calibration into one of validation. The melt boundary is located by root-finding rather than on a grid, so no discretization error enters the diagnosis. Across 231 single tracks, the model reproduces conduction-regime depth and half-width to within a few percent and underpredicts increasingly once keyholing begins. Inverting each measured depth for the absorptivity conduction would require yielding a fitting-free diagnosis: no conduction-regime track demands a non-physical value, and the inferred value converges near 0.38 against inputs of 0.27 to 0.34, whereas every keyhole-classified track demands a value above unity. Because an inferred absorptivity also absorbs unmodeled transport, downward convection was emulated as an anisotropic effective diffusivity; at the enhancement reported for Marangoni flow, no keyhole track becomes explicable. A measured Ti-6Al-4V absorptivity rise of a factor 1.9 supports the mechanism. An enthalpy-indexed correction and data-driven baselines remain alloy-specific, whereas the physics-based model retains its advantage under cross-alloy extrapolation. All findings are for single tracks on bare plates.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The high reflectivity of certain metal powders within the infrared laser range hinders the processability and quality of additively manufactured metals via laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). Here, we report a new mechanism responsible for the unusually high laser absorptivity (exceeding 70%) of high-reflectivity metals such as copper and aluminum modified with micron-sized ceramic particles. It was previously thought that the increment in the absorptivity of a composite powder is ascribed to the enhanced laser multiple reflections in the powder bed, thereby enhancing the interactions between laser beams and powder particles. However, we found that the exceptionally high laser absorptivity is attributed to the synergistic effect between metal and ceramic powders, as evidenced by combining experiments with laser ray-tracing simulations. Most laser beams reflected by the metal powders are eventually absorbed by the ceramic particles, which increases the overall laser absorptivity in a nonlinear manner. In situ monitoring of thermal energy density was conducted to identify this laser absorption mechanism during sample printing. The results from x-ray computed tomography microscopy show a significant improvement in the sample quality of L-PBF high-reflectively metallic materials. Our work provides a potential way to optimize microstructures in L-PBF high-reflectivity metallic materials.

Abstract:
The light-matter interaction of an optical beam and metal micro-particulates at the vicinity of an optical substrate surface is critical to the many fields of applied optics. Examples of impacted fields are laser-induced damage in high power laser systems, sub-wavelength laser machining of transmissive materials, and laser-target interaction in directed energy applications. We present a full-wave-based model that predicts the laser-induced plasma pressure exerted on a substrate surface as a result of light absorption in surface-bound micron-scale metal particles. The model predictions agree with experimental observation of laser-induced shallow pits, formed by plasma emission and etching from surface-bound metal micro-particulates. It provides an explanation for the prototypical side lobes observed along the pit profile, as well as for the dependence of the pit shape on the incident laser and particle parameters. Furthermore, the model highlights the significance of the interference of the incident light in the open cavity geometry formed between the micro-particle and the substrate in the resulting pit shape.

Abstract:
A critical compilation and analysis of all the available experimental data and approximation formulas for the wavelength and temperature dependences of the absorption coefficient of molten aluminum oxide in semitransparent region are presented. The main factors and the influence of physicochemical processes on the value of the absorption coefficient are considered. Special attention is focused on possible reasons for large values of absorption of the alumina melt as compared to the crystal near melting temperature. It is shown that the available data can be divided into two groups, according to the level of absorption. The first group includes the results of the research of optical properties of solid propellant combustion products, and the second group–the results of the research of single crystal melts and some other high-purity molten aluminum oxides. Along with the detailed analysis of the absorption coefficient, also a brief analysis of available data on the refractive index has been done.

Abstract:
Recent research has introduced custom beam shapes as a novel tool to stabilize laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M) and laser welding. To facilitate beam shaping in the future, new processes must be developed. However, the process development in PBF-LB/M and laser welding is time-consuming due to its empirical and iterative approach. In the center of this procedure stands the ex situ analysis of test specimens. The process development could be significantly accelerated by replacing the physical ex situ analysis with digital in situ data analysis. Therefore, this work investigates the possibility of an in situ data-based process characterization under process-near conditions for laser welding and PBF-LB/M. For this, the changes in the degree of absorption over a stepwise increase in laser power are studied for various combinations of laser spot size and beam profiles. The measurements are taken using an integrating sphere within a custom-designed testing setup. Additionally, a high-speed camera was deployed. An intensity-dependent absorption signature was found that describes the changes in the degree of absorption over an increase in mean radiation intensity independent from the beam shapes. This absorption signature contains information about the corresponding process behavior and its characteristic trend. These results are the next steps toward in situ absorption-based process characterization for accelerating process development in PBF-LB/M and laser welding.

Abstract:
Modern life and global communication would not be possible without technologically tailored thin films; they are omnipresent in daily life applications. In most cases, the films are deposited entirely at the carrying substrates in a specific processing step of the device or sample. In some cases, however, removal or modification must be performed locally, i.e., site-controlled and material selective through an additional laser processing step. For that ultrashort laser pulses with durations in the femtosecond and picosecond range can provide unique advantages and capabilities in industrially scalable schemes. This article reviews the current state of the research and corresponding industrial transfer related to the structuring of thin films by ultrashort pulsed lasers. It focuses on the pertinent historic developments, reveals the relevant physical and chemical effects, explores the ultimate limits, and discusses selected industrial and scientific applications.

Abstract:
Transparent hard and brittle (THB) materials have generated significant interest due to their excellent properties, such as wide spectral transmittance, heat resistance, chemical inactivity and high mechanical strength. To further explore the application of THB materials, it is inevitable to be confronted with a range of joining THB materials and THB material–metals. Ultrafast (UF) laser microwelding enables a new means of joining THB materials and THB material–metals, due to a localized energy deposition method, which is dominated by nonlinear absorption. This process can realize high-quality micro-zone direct joining of THB materials or THB material–metals without the assistance of a light-absorbing intermediate layer. In this paper, we review the advances in UF laser microwelding of THB materials and THB material–metals considering the last two decades, from the analysis of the interaction mechanism between UF laser and matter to the key influencing factors and practical applications of this technology. Finally, the existing problems and the future research focus of UF laser microwelding technology of THB materials and THB material–metals are discussed.

Abstract:
Challenge 3 of the 2022 NIST additive manufacturing benchmark (AM Bench) experiments asked modelers to submit predictions for solid cooling rate, liquid cooling rate, time above melt, and melt pool geometry for single and multiple track laser powder bed fusion process using moving lasers. An in-house developed A dditive M anufacturing C omputational F luid D ynamics code (AM-CFD) combined with a cylindrical heat source is implemented to accurately predict these experiments. Heuristic heat source calibration is proposed relating volumetric energy density (ψ) based on experiments available in the literature. The parameters of the heat source of the computational model are initially calibrated based on a Higher Order Proper Generalized Decomposition- (HOPGD) based surrogate model. The prediction using the calibrated heat source agrees quantitatively with NIST measurements for different process conditions (laser spot diameter, laser power, and scan speed). A scaling law based on keyhole formation is also utilized in calibrating the parameters of the cylindrical heat source and predicting the challenge experiments. In addition, an improvement on the heat source model is proposed to relate the Volumetric Energy Density (VED_σ) to the melt pool aspect ratio. The model shows further improvement in the prediction of the experimental measurements for the melt pool, including cases at higher VED_σ. Overall, it is concluded that the appropriate selection of laser heat source parameterization scheme along with the heat source model is crucial in the accurate prediction of melt pool geometry and thermal measurements while bypassing the expensive computational simulations that consider increased physics equations.

Ability to Simulate Absorption and Melt Pool Dynamics for Laser
Melting of Bare Aluminum Plate: Results and Insights from the 2022
Asynchronous AM‑Bench Challenge

Brian J. Simonds1     · Jack Tanner1 · Alexandra Artusio‑Glimpse1 · Niranjan Parab2 · Cang Zhao2,3 · Tao Sun2,4 ·
Paul A. Williams1


Received: 25 October 2023 / Accepted: 17 December 2023 / Published online: 1 February 2024
This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2024

Abstract
The 2022 Asynchronous AM-Bench challenge was designed to test the ability of simulations to accurately predict laser power
absorption as well as various melt pool behaviors (width, depth, and solidification) during laser melting of solid metal during
stationary and scanned laser illumination. In this challenge, participants were asked to predict a series of experimental out-
comes. Experimental data were obtained from a series of experiments performed at the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne
National Laboratories in 2019. These experiments combined integrating sphere radiometry with high-speed X-ray imaging,
allowing for the simultaneous recording of absolute laser power absorption and two-dimensional, projected images of the
melt pool. All challenge problems were based on experiments using bare aluminum solid metal. Participants were provided
with pertinent experimental information like laser power, scan speed, laser spot size, and material composition. Addition-
ally, participants were given absorptance and X-ray imaging data from stationary and scanned laser experiments on solid
Ti–6Al–4V that could be used for testing their models before attempting challenge problems. In total, this challenge received
56 submissions from eight different research groups for eight individual challenge problems. The data for this challenge, and
associated information, are available for download from the NIST Public Data Repository. This paper summarizes the results
from the 2022 Asynchronous AM-Bench challenge as well as discusses the lessons learned to help inform future challenges.

the initial sample surface. Laser turn-on occurs at 0 ms.

    First, considering conduction mode (Fig. 3.1a-b), at 0.35 MW/cm2, the most no-

ticeable diﬀerence is the reduced absorptance under inert conditions. In both cases,3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              69



the absorptance slowly rises with some rapid ﬂuctuations, but in argon it plateaus

to an average value of 0.21 and in air it rises to a maximum of 0.51. This diﬀerence

is explained by reduced oxidation under inert conditions. This is consistent with the

diﬀerence in appearance in the weld beads after processing. The welds performed in

air were dark brown while in argon they were bright and shiny. Considerable diﬀer-

ence is also seen in the depth measurements. In air, the center of the melt pool rises

over time to a maximum height of 83 µm, with slight ﬂuctuations throughout.  In

argon, the melt bead rises brieﬂy before showing oscillatory behaviour. In the ﬁgure,

this appears as two distinct bands of data points around −25 µm and 20 µm.

   In transition mode (Fig. 3.1c-d), at 0.46 MW/cm2, the behaviours in the two en-

vironments become more distinct. In air, we regularly observe the formation of tem-

porary, highly volatile keyholes. These appear in the ICI data as sudden increases

in depth, followed by rapid ﬂuctuations, and eventually a sudden return to the pre-

keyhole depth. Depth ﬂuctuations are likely caused by sidewall protrusions or partial

keyhole collapse, as both have the potential to limit the penetration of the ICI beam.

The absorptance increases during these temporary keyholes to a maximum of 0.56,

due to the temporary cavity formation. These shallow keyholes allow most of the

processing light to interact with the workpiece multiple times due to reﬂections. It is

interesting that even with the increased absorptance, the incident beam has suﬃcient

energy to form a keyhole but not to sustain it.  Surface tension pressure has been

proposed as the likely cause for this behaviour [25]. As irradiance increases through

the transition mode in air (0.44 MW/cm2 to 0.49 MW/cm2), the frequency and du-

ration of temporary keyholes increases until a consistent keyhole can be maintained

[22]. In argon, it was possible to observe this behaviour, albeit less frequently. More3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              70





Figure 3.1: Time-resolved depth and absorptance data from spot welds: (a) in argon
at 0.35 MW/cm2, (b) in air at 0.35 MW/cm2, (c) in argon at 0.46 MW/cm2, (d) in
air at 0.46 MW/cm2, (e) in argon at 0.58 MW/cm2, (f) in air at 0.58 MW/cm2.


often, a keyhole would not form at all and instead the depth and absorptance would

oscillate, similar to what was seen in conduction mode. This seemingly high vari-

ability between forming temporary keyholes or strong surface oscillations occurs over

the narrow processing window from 0.45 MW/cm2 to 0.52 MW/cm2. The oscillating

behaviour is analyzed in greater detail in Sec. 3.4.3.

   In keyhole mode (Fig. 3.1e-f), at 0.58 MW/cm2, the diﬀerences between air and

argon conditions are reduced. For both environments, this irradiance is suﬃcient to

quickly initiate keyhole formation and keep it open for the full 10 ms pulse. In argon,3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              71



the keyhole growth rate is lower and does not reach the same maximum depth as in air

for identical irradiances. The measured maximum absorptance is similarly reduced.

These diﬀerences are expected, as oxygen content in the assist gas has been shown to

increase laser cutting speed [26] and improve the weldability of copper [27]. In both

cases, an increase in initial absorptance due to oxidation was cited as the reason for

these beneﬁts. This claim seems to be conﬁrmed by our data, as the weld in air has

increased initial absorptance and greater achieved depths for the same laser exposure.

Another eﬀect that may play a part is the change in convective melt pool dynamics in

inert environments. Speciﬁcally, the Marangoni ﬂow in laser welding of stainless steel

has been shown to ﬂow inward towards the center of the melt pool in the presence of

high concentrations of oxygen and switch to outward ﬂow when oxygen concentration

is signiﬁcantly reduced [28].


3.4.2  Average depth and coupling eﬃciency in argon and in air


Time-averaged data, while only giving limited information about the dynamics of the

process, are still useful for distinguishing thresholds between conduction and keyhole

mode and for comparing general trends between processing parameters. From the

time-resolved data shown in Sec. 3.4.1, it is straightforward to calculate the average

absorptance (coupling eﬃciency) and average depth for each irradiance, as shown in

Fig. 3.2.

   For coupling eﬃciency, there is a striking gap at low irradiance due to lack of

oxidation in inert environments. The largest diﬀerence is observed at an irradiance

of 0.23 MW/cm2, with argon and air environments giving coupling eﬃciencies of 0.08

and 0.42, respectively. As irradiance increases the argon coupling eﬃciency rises until3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              72



the point where we start to observe temporary keyholes (the end of the conduction

mode). In the absence of oxide formation this can be explained by the temperature

dependence of absorptance [29, 30]. Over the same range in air, the measured cou-

pling eﬃciency is relatively stable and even drops slightly before the transition mode

starts, suggesting that oxide formation has a stronger inﬂuence than temperature on

absorptance under these conditions. The slight drop may be caused by irradiance

becoming high enough for oxide vapourization, but not yet high enough to gener-

ate suﬃcient recoil pressure to open a keyhole. Overall, conduction mode in argon

compared to air has a 50 % ± 11 % reduction in coupling eﬃciency.

   The main diﬀerences that occur in the transition regime between argon and air

were described above alongside the time-resolved data, but here the diﬀerence in

keyhole threshold is better displayed. At 0.45 MW/cm2, both environments start to

allow temporary keyholes to form. By 0.52 MW/cm2, spot welds in air consistently

form sustained keyholes. In argon, we do not observe this until 0.58 MW/cm2. The

coupling eﬃciencies measured at these thresholds are 0.58 for air and 0.59 for argon.

These values are obviously similar, but also close to the expected Fresnel absorption

value that one would obtain from two reﬂections oﬀa liquid steel surface [9, 31, 32].

This may imply that regardless of processing conditions the start of keyhole mode

is the formation of a shallow cavity that supports two reﬂections (e.g., a cone with

an aspect ratio of 1). This condition has been predicted in models for moving welds

[25, 33].

   In keyhole mode, the coupling eﬃciencies in both environments start to approach

similar behaviour. In this regime, factors that dominate absorptance in conduction

and transition mode are now dwarfed by the geometric eﬀects of keyholes and the3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              73





Figure 3.2: Time-averaged data for (a) coupling eﬃciency and (b) average depth, for
both argon and air environments.


multiple reﬂections they facilitate.  Interestingly, the coupling eﬃciencies are closer3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              74



than one would expect when considering that the argon spot welds have dispropor-

tionately lower average depth in this regime.  Firstly, this may simply be because

absorptance has a reduced sensitivity to depth as depth increases [7]. At a certain

point, more reﬂections will have a negligible eﬀect on the absorptance, so keyholes

over a range of depths can all give similar absorptance. Another possibility is that

the shape of the keyhole is generally diﬀerent between the two environments, allowing

the shallower keyholes in argon to give similar absorptance as those deeper ones in

air. Regardless of the exact mechanisms, the coupling eﬃciency in keyhole mode in

argon compared to air is reduced by only 8 % ± 3 %.


3.4.3  Time-frequency data from transition mode in argon


Time-resolved data from the transition mode in argon suggests oscillatory behaviour,

but the relationship between frequency of depth and absorptance ﬂuctuations is not

obvious from simple inspection of Fig. 3.1c. We use a short-time Fourier transform

(STFT) to quantify oscillation frequencies of the time-resolved depth and absorptance

data and see how they evolve in time. STFTs cannot be performed on sparse data sets,

and since ICI experiences occasional signal loss in this regime due to oﬀ-axis specular

reﬂections, gaps in the depth measurements are linearly interpolated before frequency

analysis. STFTs were performed on depth and absorptance data independently, using

a Hann window with a length of 1 ms and 50 % overlap (to ensur

obvious from simple inspection of Fig. 3.1c. We use a short-time Fourier transform

(STFT) to quantify oscillation frequencies of the time-resolved depth and absorptance

data and see how they evolve in time. STFTs cannot be performed on sparse data sets,

and since ICI experiences occasional signal loss in this regime due to oﬀ-axis specular

Fig. 3.1c. In both the absorptance and depth spectrograms there is a distinct curve

that starts near 15 kHz and decreases to 10 kHz over the weld duration. There are also

fainter curves at multiples of these frequency values. These higher harmonics suggest

that the oscillations are not perfectly sinusoidal. Also notable from the spectrograms

is the width of the fundamental frequency peaks. These peaks are modeled well by3.4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION                              76



Gaussian functions and all have full width at half maximum close to 2 kHz.  This

gives a good estimate on the frequency resolution of this method, although the ﬁt

uncertainties on the center frequency positions are much lower (less than 10 Hz).

   Figure 3.3c plots the peak frequency (found by Gaussian ﬁtting) as a function of

time for both depth and absorptance. This shows more clearly how the fundamental

frequency decreases over time, which is expected to occur as the melt pool volume

grows [34]. The analogy of a vibrating drumhead is useful: a larger surface area drum

has a lower resonance frequency. The second point is that the frequency of oscillations

in depth and absorptance, which are measured independently, evolve together with

similar values. This suggests that these non-keyhole surface oscillations are directly

responsible for the oscillations in absorptance.

   As mentioned in Sec. 3.4.1, we observe these strong surface oscillations throughout

the transition mode in argon, but sometimes a repeated trial at the same irradiance

will show temporary keyhole formation. Being so close to the threshold of keyhole

formation, it is possible that the amplitude of the absorptance oscillations may dic-

tate when these temporary keyholes form. As other work has shown, the fundamental

frequency of the melt pool can be driven by modulating the laser beam at the same

frequency to assist in laser drilling [35]. Here we show that driving these surface oscil-

lations may not work only by mechanical resonance, but also by dynamic increases in

energy coupling. This may open the possibility of ﬁne control over keyhole formation

(or suppression) by monitoring and exploiting surface mode oscillations.3.5. CONCLUSION                                            77



3.5  Conclusion


By implementing ICI and ISR simultaneously to monitor laser spot welding of AISI

316 stainless steel, we have revealed unique insights into the underlying physics of

laser-metal interaction. We showed that processing in argon compared to air sig-

niﬁcantly reduces coupling eﬃciency in conduction mode due to the lack of oxide

formation. We observed that transition mode melt pools in argon undergo well-

deﬁned surface oscillations, decrease in frequency from 15 kHz to 10 kHz over time,

and sometimes form temporary keyholes. These surface oscillations also produced

highly correlated oscillations in absorptance. In a range of irradiance where sustain-

able keyholes could be formed, time-resolved and time-averaged data for spot welds

in argon and in air become more similar, providing further evidence that multiple

reﬂections is the dominant factor that inﬂuences absorptance in keyhole mode. These

observations will be valuable for development of models and active control schemes,

highlighting the importance of hybrid monitoring tools that measure multiple aspects

of the process simultaneously.

4.1  Abstract


The integration of aluminum parts for purposes of lightweighting requires joining alu-

minum to steel. This process is infamously diﬃcult, due to the poor laser weldability

of aluminum and the brittle intermetallic phases that form when the two metals mix.

Precise control of the process is enabled by deep understanding of the underlying

physics. To aid in this eﬀort, we collect simultaneous time-resolved keyhole depth

measured by inline coherent imaging and absolute absorptance measured by integrat-

ing sphere radiometry, during spot welds on 6061 aluminum, 316 stainless steel, and

on both materials in lap weld conﬁguration. We ﬁnd that laser welding through steel

into aluminum carried the beneﬁts of steel keyhole welding (laser absorptance near or

above 0.9, predictable keyhole formation), while also leading to more stable keyholes

(standard deviation of keyhole depth was reduced by 50 % compared to steel welding

alone). In comparison, laser welding through aluminum into steel faced similar prob-

lems as aluminum welding alone, such as unpredictable keyhole formation and large

ﬂuctuations in depth and absorptance (more than twice as large compared to steel

alone).



4.2  Introduction


Lightweight manufacturing, integrating lighter materials into existing or new designs

without sacriﬁcing strength, is an important topic in the aerospace and automotive

industries. One aspiration of this ﬁeld is the inclusion of aluminum parts into pre-

dominantly steel assemblies. This faces the inevitable challenge of joining the two

dissimilar metals together. Laser welding is one technique that has hopes to achieve

this, but has historically faced many hurdles [2–6].4.2. INTRODUCTION                                         86

cially due to its high thermal conductivity, high thermal expansion, low viscosity, and

high reﬂectance at ﬁbre laser wavelengths. Steel is comparatively easy to weld, but

that matters little when attempting to fuse it with aluminum. In dissimilar mate-

rials welding, diﬀerences in melting temperature, density, and other thermophysical

properties make the system more diﬃcult to control and predict than single material

welding. One crucial problem is the formation of brittle intermetallic phases as the

melted metals mix, which greatly aﬀect the strength of the ﬁnal joint.

are best validated by time-resolved measurements, but there has yet to be signiﬁcant

inclusion of such data.

development of steel-aluminum laser welding. We do this by combining inline coherent

imaging (ICI), to measure melt pool surface height/depth with micrometer precision

at 200 kHz in industrial settings [11–13], and integrating sphere radiometry (ISR), to

measure absolute absorptance of laser power during the process at speeds up to 1 MHz

[14–18]. By observing both depth and absorptance during a variety of steel-aluminum

lap welds, we can provide insight into melt pool and energy-coupling behaviour as a

keyhole crosses between materials.4.3. METHODS                                               87



4.3  Methods


4.3.1  Processing laser


Laser spot welding is performed using a 1 kW Yb-doped ﬁbre laser (multimode) with a

100 µm core delivery ﬁbre. A 150 mm focal length lens is used to focus the processing

laser beam to a 1/e2 spot size of 238 µm. The focused beam has an M 2 value of

9.8 and a Rayleigh length of 4.23 mm. In this experiment, the laser is operated with

powers ranging from 564 W to 974 W, conﬁrmed to within 3 % with a power meter

(PRIMES). The laser is ﬁred to produce single pulses of 10 ms nominal duration. The

actual pulse durations range from 9.975 ms to 9.992 ms depending on the laser power

setting, conﬁrmed with a photodiode measuring scattered light. The laser pulses are

top hat-shaped with rise times shorter than 75 µs.


4.3.2  Simultaneous inline coherent imaging and integrating sphere ra-

      diometry


Inline coherent imaging (ICI) is low coherence interferometry implemented collinearly

with the high-power processing beam [11–13]. The ICI system used in this work can

extract 1-dimensional sample height at a rate of 200 kHz, with an axial resolution of

15 µm (minimum axial distance between two interfaces that can be distinguished in a

single axial scan) and a single-point measurement repeatability of 0.6 µm (limited by

the stability of the ﬁbre interferometer). Integrating sphere radiography (ISR) is a

technique that uses an integrating sphere to measure oﬀ-axis scattered light from laser

illumination in order to calculate absolute absorptance [14–18]. The ISR system used

in the present work measures scattered light in the sphere with a photodiode with a

rise time of 4.4 µs. Absolute calibration is performed by ﬁring laser pulses with known4.3. METHODS                                               88

Samples of 316 stainless steel (SS) and 6061 aluminum are sanded with a repeatable

Through time-resolved measurements of keyhole depth and absolute absorptance, we
