Chapter 5


Integrating sphere radiometry

absorptance measurements during

laser powder bed fusion of

AlSi10Mg in a commercial build

environment




Troy R. Allen1, Sagar Patel2, Madison K. Reed1, Peyman Alimehr2, Mihaela Vlasea2,

James M. Fraser1



1Queen’s University, 64 Bader Lane, Kingston, Ontario K7L 3N6, Canada

2University of Waterloo, 137 Glasgow St, Kitchener, Ontario N2G 4X8, Canada5.1. ABSTRACT                                             103



This article is soon to be submitted.



5.1  Abstract


Metal additive manufacturing (AM) is promising to revolutionize how we make things,

from lightweight aerospace parts to medical implants tailored to speciﬁc patients.

However, widespread adoption and regulatory certiﬁcation is impaired by our lim-

ited understanding of the fundamental laser-powder interaction that underpins metal

AM techniques. Process optimization for each new part design remains a slow and

costly undertaking, as even small changes to laser power, beam size, scan pattern, or

powder size and shape, can lead to dramatic diﬀerences in ﬁnal part quality. Com-

puter models have been developed with the goal of accurately predicting acceptable

parameter windows before starting to invest materials, but these models have been

overwhelmingly trained on post-build investigations (e.g., cross-sections, CT scans),

that provide little to no information on the physics driving the dynamic process.

Even the laser energy coupling into the metal powder, the foremost quantity needed

to predict build behaviour with high ﬁdelity, is often treated as an average value

measured from bulk materials.  Recent literature has proven this approach to be

wrong, ﬁnding that:  (i) laser energy coupling is a highly dynamic quantity and (ii)

materials in powder form do not inherit their bulk properties.  Integrating sphere

radiometry, a technique capable of time-resolved (260 kHz) calibrated absorptance

measurements, is implemented in a commercial AM machine to uncover the under-

lying physics of laser energy coupling in real build conditions. The eﬀect of powder

on absorptance of AlSi10Mg is clearly displayed by contrasting measurements on

machined (0.06 ± 0.02), bare AM-built (0.22 ± 0.05), and powder covered AM-built5.2. INTRODUCTION                                        104



substrates (0.72 ± 0.05) in conduction mode conditions. By melting and/or removing

powder from the laser path, hatching and denudation is seen to reduce absorptance

in multi-track AM by up to 40 % compared to the ﬁrst line. Rich insights gained from

these measurements should inform future model development and encourage wider

use of ISR as an investigative research tool.



5.2  Introduction


Laser-based powder-bed fusion (L-PBF), a common branch of metal additive manu-

facturing (AM), is promising to revolutionize how we make things, from lightweight

aerospace parts to medical implants tailored to speciﬁc patients [1–3]. By repeatedly

scanning a high-power laser beam over a re-coatable bed of metal powder, L-PBF

allows customized complex parts to be built directly from 3D CAD models.  This

technology will have direct impacts on global manufacturing sustainability, because

in comparison to traditional metal manufacturing techniques, AM comes with: im-

provements in energy consumption and production cost, produces less material waste

and CO2 emission, and has the ﬂexibility of a shorter supply chain [4, 5]. Though the

list of industries that could beneﬁt from AM is long, widespread adoption faces the

hurdle of standardization—especially in safety-critical applications such as aerospace

and medical—because regulators are not yet convinced that AM processes are funda-

mentally well-understood [6, 7].

   One often- and long-cited reason for the lack of fundamental AM knowledge is

a shortage of in situ measurements of the process [1, 4, 8–13]. Such measurements

could directly probe the mechanisms behind common defects and help develop miti-

gation strategies, or they can be used to train and validate the time-resolved ﬁdelity5.2. INTRODUCTION                                        105



of large computational models. However, making such measurements is diﬃcult. The

environment around a high-power laser beam incident on a layer of metal powder

is a complex system involving light-matter interaction, heat transfer, phase changes

from solid to liquid to gas, and ﬂuid mechanics [14]. Consider the general opacity of

metal combined with fast (kHz or higher) dynamics on the µm-scale, and it becomes

apparent why in situ observations have been historically passed over for ex situ in-

vestigations. Nevertheless, great strides have been made in recent years to address

this shortage of time-resolved data.

   Due to the importance of solving the challenges, considerable work has been in-

vested to develop in situ sensors and measurement systems for AM in the last several

years, targeting diﬀerent phenomena with varying levels of directness, precision, and

robustness. The most direct methods typically require the largest footprint and most

sophisticated equipment, and tend to necessitate highly constrained build geometries

making them incompatible with large-scale commercial AM systems.  Instead, the

AM process is emulated in a reduced capacity on bench-top setups, often limiting

study scopes to single-layer or single-track experiments [15]. The most extreme ex-

ample of this class of in situ measurements comes from high-speed x-ray imaging at

synchrotron facilities, which produce unparalleled high-speed cross-sectional views of

the AM process using incredibly specialized and expensive equipment and include

strict restrictions to single-track experiments on narrow samples [16–21]. On the

other end of the ﬁdelity scale, many commercial AM machines oﬀer proprietary sen-

sor suites built into the build chamber. This has the advantage of making in situ

measurements during the entire build process, but these sensors are typically indirect5.2. INTRODUCTION                                        106



in nature [10, 22, 23]. An example would be a passive photodiode measuring scat-

tered light levels inside the chamber with the goal of correlating steady-state signal to

nominal build behaviour or certain signatures to defect events. Due to the unwieldy

amount of data collected over the course of a whole build, some methods achieve data

reduction by integrating over space and/or time. Considering the highly dynamic na-

ture of the laser-powder melting process (temperature gradients of up to 3000 °C over

as little as 10 microns, morphology changes on µs timescales), sensors that employ

averaging can completely miss signatures relevant to the melting process. If the data

is preserved in its full time resolution, researchers often resort to machine learning

(ML) to ga

## 3. allen2023sheddinglighton pages 120-124 (Context ID: pqac-00000037)

would be a passive photodiode measuring scat-

tered light levels inside the chamber with the goal of correlating steady-state signal to

nominal build behaviour or certain signatures to defect events. Due to the unwieldy

amount of data collected over the course of a whole build, some methods achieve data

reduction by integrating over space and/or time. Considering the highly dynamic na-

ture of the laser-powder melting process (temperature gradients of up to 3000 °C over

as little as 10 microns, morphology changes on µs timescales), sensors that employ

averaging can completely miss signatures relevant to the melting process. If the data

is preserved in its full time resolution, researchers often resort to machine learning

(ML) to gain useful insight from such large data sets in a reasonable time, but such

research is still in early stages and lacks best practices for ML model development and

supervision [13, 15, 23, 24]. There seems to be unavoidable trade oﬀs between spe-

cialized, open, direct in situ measurements, the ability to implement them in relevant

commercial-grade AM processes, and the capacity to handle the resulting amount of

data.

   This patchwork landscape of measurement techniques leads to gaps in our under-

standing of the underlying physics of large-scale, multi-layer AM. These gaps create

problems when it comes to training computational models. A striking example comes

from the treatment of laser energy coupling, where absorptivity measured on polished

bulk samples is commonly used as a constant model input. The coupling of laser en-

ergy into the metal powder during AM is the vital ﬁrst physical process from which

everything else follows, and to treat it as a material constant, ignoring the dynamics

introduced by powder and melt pool geometry, is a gross simpliﬁcation [25–30]. One

can take hints from the laser welding community, where the formation of keyholes5.2. INTRODUCTION                                        107



(or vapour depressions) has been known for decades to increase absorptance (more

than double compared to ﬂat surface) by allowing multiple reﬂections of the laser

beam [31–33]. Some might claim that stable AM processes do not produce keyholes

and cite the lack of porosity as evidence, but in situ x-ray measurements proved that

shallow vapour depressions are created within stable AM parameter windows [34] and

unintented deep keyholes can form at turnaround points in raster scan patterns [19].

The eﬀect of powder beds as a scatterer and vehicle for multiple reﬂections is also

well-known [26, 29, 30, 35–37]. Therefore, dynamic energy coupling is a crucial yet

understudied aspect of AM that demands more research attention.

   Direct measurements of energy coupling dedicated to AM are rare, and have not

yet met the criteria of high-quality, high-speed, and close to commercial-level. Trapp

et al. used in situ micro calorimetry to measure temperature increase in single track

AM experiments on steel and aluminum powder and thereby calculate average ab-

sorptivity [38]. The average absorptivity measurements were used to identify process

regimes (conduction, transition, and keyhole mode) as a function of laser power, for

diﬀerent materials and scan speeds. This work also provided valuable insight into the

quantitative eﬀects of powder layers compared to bare plate samples on absorptiv-

ity. However, this method is not time-resolved, and the requirements for a thermally

isolated sample and integrated thermocouples would likely make it challenging to

operate in a commercial AM machine over multiple layers. Brandau et al. used inte-

grating sphere spectroscopy to characterize absorbance for many diﬀerent powders in

non-melting conditions [39]. This work is useful for understanding the initial laser ab-

sorptance of virgin powder, but previous research with high-speed video and coherent

imaging has shown that the vast majority of an AM build involves light interacting5.2. INTRODUCTION                                        108



with a very diﬀerent metal environment (due mostly to hatching and powder de-

nudation) that could range from highly absorbing (e.g., due to multiple scattering in

powder or keyholes) to highly reﬂective (e.g., specular reﬂection from liquid metal

surfaces or substrate revealed by denudation) [40–43]. Integrating sphere radiometry

(ISR) is an old technique recently applied to laser-material processing that uses in-

expensive, 3D-printed spheres with full customization of optical ports. With careful

calibration, ISR can make fast absolute absorptance measurements (typically 100 kHz

or higher) by measuring the amount of laser light scattered from a sample during laser

irradiation. In addition to stand-alone bench-top experiments [25, 26, 44–46], ISR has

previously been combined with inline coherent imaging (ICI) in an industrial laser

welding cell for simultaneous measurements of depth and absorptance [47–49], and

has been integrated into a synchrotron beam line for simultaneous high-speed x-ray

does not mean the sphere should be as large as possible. As the surface area of the

sphere is increased, the ﬂux density incident on the sphere walls, including the output

ontact between the powder and sphere while also avoiding

any direct gap for light to escape, all experiments in this work are done on a raised

substrate layer 5 mm into the sphere. This also has the important advantage that

measurement is done for powder layers on real AM-built substrates thus mimicking

real build conditions. It is also critical that the calibration target and samples used

for measurement are placed in the same position, so calibration targets for this work5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             115



were cut to roughly match the substrate size so they ﬁt inside the sample port.

   Previous implementations of ISR in laser-based manufacturing experiments have

predominantly been carried out at normal incidence, and therefore included an ad-

ditional photodiode intended to measure back-reﬂections of the laser beam through

the top of the sphere (which commonly occurred at the start of laser-melting exper-

iments) [25]. Adding this additional photodiode would have been impossible in this

commercial additive system. This is one of the original reasons behind the decision

to process at 11°, as described above.  In this experiment, the presence of powder

should limit specular reﬂection from the sample in general, and if they occur, direct

reﬂections should tend toward the opposite sphere wall. This did come with concerns

about burning the interior coating with high-power specular reﬂections, but inspec-

tion of the sphere during and after the experiments revealed no visible damage, and

there was no systematic degradation in sphere signal observed over the course of the

experiment.

   The output port includes a 2 mm hole with half of a FC/PC ﬁbre port mounted on

the outside. A multi-mode ﬁbre with a 200 µm core and numerical aperture (NA) of

0.22 (Thorlabs M122L05) is connected to this ﬁbre port, delivering the tip of the ﬁbre

ﬂush with the interior sphere wall. The NA of the ﬁbre informed the design of the

baﬄe, ensuring only light that has reﬂected multiple times can enter the ﬁbre. The

ﬁbre passes through an airtight port on a custom cap for an unused powder exhaust

port on the Renishaw AM 400.  Light from the ﬁbre enters free space through a

terminated ﬁbre adapter (Thorlabs SM1FC) and passes through an assembly of ﬁlters

before reaching the detector. The ﬁrst is an ND 0.5 ﬁlter (measured as 0.500 ± 0.001)

that compensates for the lower powers used in the calibration process (explained in5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             116



Sec. 5.3.3). The second is a 1070 nm laser line band-pass ﬁlter that ensures only light

from the processing laser is measured by the photodiode (e.g., eliminating blackbody

radiation). Any blackbody radiation near the processing laser wavelength is estimated

to be orders of magnitude lower in power compared to the scattered laser light, and

so is considered negligible. The optical path from the ﬁbre adapter to the detector

is stable as all the components are held together by threaded mounts and screwed

onto the photodiode directly. For the ﬁxed distance from ﬁbre tip to detector, the

max spot size of the beam from the ﬁbre ﬁlls most of the detector area. When the

ND ﬁlter is removed during calibration, an empty optical mount of the same size is

put in its place to maintain this constant distance. The rise time of the photodiode

(Thorlabs PDA100A2) at the gain setting used in this work (30 dB) is 3.8 µs. The

output of the photodiode is recorded by an oscilloscope (Tektronix DPO-3034) at a

time resolution of 1 µs. Data acquisition is handled by a custom LabVIEW program.


Measuring the input power


ISR measurements require accurate and speciﬁc knowledge of input laser power as a

function of time. This is typically gained through separate measurements of laser en-

ergy and pulse shape for every individual parameter set planned for the experiment.

Photodiodes can provide time-resolved intensity proﬁles, but since incident powers

must be limited to avoid damage, they are not usually compatible with absolute

measurements for the powers required in AM. Power/energy meters can withstand

such high powers, but typically do not give high temporal resolution. Combining the

two allows time-resolved calibrated measurement. In its most straightforward imple-

mentation, the laser would be controlled to generate a top hat of speciﬁc duration5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             117



and resolved by the photodiode. Since the integral of this trace is pulse energy, the

absolute scale can be calibrated using an energy meter to capture the pulse energy.

  We ﬁnd that to achieve similar results in commercial AM systems is more compli-

cated, particularly in single point exposure systems like the Renishaw AM 400 used

in this study. Typical AM control software was not intended for this sort of measure-

ment so does not allow the detailed control described above. In addition, the system

generates a more complicated intensity waveform than just a square wave; that is,

pulse intensity decreases between pulses but does not reach zero. The eﬀective mod-

ulation frequency of this laser output exceeded the speciﬁed maximum frequency of

the available power meter, so it was not possible to directly measure total energy

contained in a typical pulse train.

  A three-step measurement system was devised to overcome these challenges: (1)

measure calibrated power for the long pulse emission, (2) capture the uncalibrated

intensity trace for each parameter set used for the multi-track experiments, and (3)

capture uncalibrated intensity traces of both short and long pulses together from

the same power set point. From (3), the peak intensity of the short pulses can be

compared to the top hat intensity of the long pulses. Then from (1) and (2), the

calibrated average power from the long pulse can be scaled appropriately to the peak

power of the short pulses, thereby producing a calibrated pulse train of power as a

function of time.

   Average laser power was measured for 1 s to 2 s long pulses using a commercial

power meter (PRIMES Cube, Germany). The meter was mounted in the center of

the build plate (location marked using the laser) and the build plate was lowered to

−300 mm to achieve the speciﬁed minimum spot size on the absorbing surface of the5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             118



power meter of 5 mm (conﬁrmed using photosensitive paper). The Renishaw AM 400

was operated at an access level that allowed manual ﬁring of the laser at any power

setting with minimum duration of 1 s. This mode is only used for calibration and

servicing of the machine and is not used at any future point in the experiment. The

power meter also has an energy threshold of 50 J for accurate measurement, so some

of the lower power settings needed 2 s exposures.

   Pulse train shapes for the experiment were captured next. Ideally, the laser would

be kept stationary, defocused signiﬁcantly, and incident on a diﬀuse target. Then,

a photodiode placed nearby could passively measure time-resolved laser output with

no other variables aﬀecting signal level.  However, due to constraints of the AM

machine interface, it was unfeasible to program the laser to ﬁre a stationary pulse

train to match relevant pulse trains for the experiment. A workaround was developed

where the machine was programmed to “build” tracks that matched all the same

parameters to be used in the multi-track experiments (length, exposure time, point

distance, hatch spacing, etc.) except it was positioned in the center of the build plate.

The scanning beam would eﬀect the signal measured at a stationary photodiode, so

there was a now a need to eliminate, or at least mitigate, this positional dependence.

A diﬀuse gold target (later used for calibration) was placed in the path of the laser

beam, and the bottom half of the integrating sphere was placed upside-down on top

of the target, with the ﬁbre installed. The build plate was again lowered to −300 mm

to defocus the beam. The result is a ﬁbre-coupled free-space reﬂective diﬀuser. The

long dimension of the bottom sphere opening is aligned in the direction of the laser

scan pattern. Even 300 mm below the focal plane, the laser beam scans through the

opening of the sphere and hits the gold target, scattering diﬀusely inside the half5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             119



sphere and coupling into the ﬁbre to be detected. This did not completely remove

the spatial dependence on the signal, as the signal did drop slightly in the middle of

the scan path, but since this was highly reproducible it could be normalized after the

fact. After normalizing to achieve relative uniformity in peak height, the measured

signal still needs to be related to the measured power, and this is achieved by the

next measurement.

the spatial dependence on the signal, as the signal did drop slightly in the middle of

the scan path, but since this was highly reproducible it could be normalized after the

fact. After normalizing to achieve relative uniformity in peak height, the measured

signal still needs to be related to the measured power, and this is achieved by the

next measurement.

    Lastly, the two previous measurements are linked by comparing peak signal in

short pulses to average signal in long pulse operation. To be clear, the goal is to

relate the uncalibrated, normalized laser output traces captured in step 2 to the

calibrated laser output power measured in step 1. The physical set up is the same as

the pulse train measurements above. Signal level from 5 pulses each of 30 µs, 60 µs,

80 µs, 100 µs, and most of a single 1 s pulse at the same set point power were captured

in the same measurement window. Importantly, the pulses are all aimed very close

to the center of the target (within 30 µm), so there is no spatial dependence in the

signal. There was a clear and consistent ratio between the peak signal of the short

pulses and the mean steady-state signal from the long pulse. In this case, the peak

signal from the short pulses was taken as the mean of the 10 highest points within

the range of 20 points centered on the peak value. The ratio of peak signal level to

steady-state signal level for the same power is 99.98 % for 100 µs pulses, 99.67 % for

80 µs pulses, 98.9 % for 60 µs pulses, and 92.7 % for 30 µs pulses. These ratios were

used to convert the raw signal of the pulse trains measured in step 2 to calculated

input power as a function of time.5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             120



Measuring the reﬂected power inside the integrating sphere


Measurements of reﬂected power during AM experiments are made possible by cal-

ibrating the integrating sphere. This was achieved by measuring sphere photodiode

signal while hitting a diﬀuse sample of known reﬂectance with pulses of known laser

power. A diﬀuse reﬂective calibration target (Infragold, Labsphere, USA), with re-

ﬂectance at 1070 nm of 93 %, was placed in one of the planned substrate positions

before printing. The calibration sample was cut to match the size of the substrates,

so it ﬁlled the entire sample port and sat at the same height inside the sphere. With

the sphere installed on the target, a series of 9 pulses was ﬁred at 75 locations (675

total pulses) arranged in a grid pattern that sparsely covered the full extent of the

target surface. By sampling many positions on the calibration target, the combined

uncertainty due to variations of the target reﬂectivity and spatial non-uniformity of

the sphere were incorporated into the calibration. The signals generated by these

pulses were measured over a range of 8 powers from 45 W–65 W. This procedure was

repeated for each substrate position, but due to an error in the procedure one of the

attempts is discarded. The slopes of the resulting linear relationships for incident

power versus photodiode signal were slightly diﬀerent for each position, so all data

were combined together so that the variance from diﬀerent calibrations would factor

into the uncertainty in the ﬁnal linear ﬁt (Fig. 5.2). This ﬁt gave a slope representing

power as a function of photodiode signal, called the calibration factor, C = 569 W/V.

   One challenge in calibrating an integrating sphere for laser-based manufacturing

experiments is avoiding damage to the calibration target while still achieving compa-

rable signal levels expected for the real experiment. The main method to solve this

involves lowering laser power as much as necessary to avoid damage to the calibration5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             121





Figure 5.2: Calibration data used to determine relationship between measured signal
and reﬂected power. The calibration is performed with input power as the indepen-
dent variable, but the important output is the slope of power as a function of signal.
Each circle represents the average signal measured from 75 diﬀerent locations on the
target. The diﬀerent colours denote the three series of measurements from diﬀerent
substrate locations. The black dashed line represents the ﬁt from the linear regres-
sion (including all data points). It is extended to zero to show that the ﬁt is forced
through the origin.


target, and then adding a ND ﬁlter to the optical path from the sphere to the photodi-

ode during the actual experiment. This eﬀectively lowers the signal measured during

experiment, adds some uncertainty due to the ND value of the ﬁlter, but overall low-

ers uncertainty by bringing the signal level close to the level reached in calibration.

In this work, the small spot size of the laser posed a further challenge, so in addition

to lowering power and reducing exposure time to 30 µs, the beam was defocused to

a 207 µm spot size. It was conﬁrmed experimentally that changing the spot size did

not have a signiﬁcant eﬀect on measured signal from the calibration target. Another

unforeseen issue came in the form of ﬁrst pulses being shortened from their nominal5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             122

ﬁrst 2-3 pulses in a pulse train, so will not have any signiﬁcant impact on full AM

builds or even single-track experiments. However, the calibration procedure is more

sensitive to this issue since it relies on a series of pulses in a grid, where each new

point on the grid would start a new pulse train. To solve this, each point on the grid

contains a train of 9 pulses and only the average of the last 5 pulses are used in the

calibration calculation.

cover the method to use measurements of input power and reﬂected power to calculate

absolute absorptance.


Absorptance calculation


The time-dependent absorbed power, PA(t), is calculated from time-resolved measure-

ments of input power, P0(t), and in situ integrating sphere reﬂected power, PR(t).

Assuming no transmission through the sample, this is calculated using the following

energy balance:


                             PA(t) = P0(t) −PR(t).                            (5.1)


   P0(t) is found by normalizing the amplitude of the measured pulse train signals,

Spt(t), to 1 and then multiplying by the measured average power for that power5.3. MATERIAL AND METHODS                             123



setting, PAV G, and a factor, M, such that the peaks of the pulse train reach the

correct peak power,


                           P0(t) = M × PAV G × Snorm(t).                        (5.2)


   The values of M were determined by dividing the peak signal of the short pulses

by the average signal of a long, square pulse at the same power (Section 5.3.3). This

varied by pulse duration, but showed no trend with set point power, so an average

value was taken for each pulse duration. The M values and uncertainty are listed in

Table 5.1. The uncertainty reported in Table 5.1 corresponds to standard deviation

from multiple measurements.

power meter measurements.

                     60                    0.989 ± 0.001
                     80                  0.9967 ± 0.0005
                     100                 0.9998 ± 0.0004


   Before measuring power inside the sphere, the calibration factor, C, needs to be

calculated. Following the experimental procedure for calibration described above, a

linear regression of peak signal, Scal, to reﬂected power, Pcal, is performed.  Pcal is

Abstract:
The use of components fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) requires the development of processing parameters that can produce high-quality material. Manipulating the most commonly identified critical build parameters (e.g., laser power, laser scan speed, and layer thickness) on LPBF equipment can generate acceptable parts for established materials and moderately intricate part geometries. The need to fabricate increasingly complex parts from unique materials drives the limited research into LPBF process control using underutilized parameters, such as atmosphere composition and pressure. As presented in this review, manipulating atmosphere composition and pressure in laser beam welding has been shown to expand processing windows and produce higher-quality welds. The similarities between laser beam welding and laser-based AM processes suggest that this atmosphere control research could be effectively adapted for LPBF, an area that has not been widely explored. Tailoring this research for LPBF has significant potential to reveal novel processing regimes. This review presents the current state of the art in atmosphere research for laser beam welding and LPBF, with a focus on studies exploring cover gas composition and pressure, and concludes with an outlook on future LPBF atmosphere control systems.

Abstract:
Keyhole porosity is a key concern in laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF), potentially impacting component fatigue life. However, some keyhole porosity formation mechanisms, e.g., keyhole fluctuation, collapse and bubble growth and shrinkage, remain unclear. Using synchrotron X-ray imaging we reveal keyhole and bubble behaviour, quantifying their formation dynamics. The findings support the hypotheses that: (i) keyhole porosity can initiate not only in unstable, but also in the transition keyhole regimes created by high laser power-velocity conditions, causing fast radial keyhole fluctuations (2.5–10 kHz); (ii) transition regime collapse tends to occur part way up the rear-wall; and (iii) immediately after keyhole collapse, bubbles undergo rapid growth due to pressure equilibration, then shrink due to metal-vapour condensation. Concurrent with condensation, hydrogen diffusion into the bubble slows the shrinkage and stabilises the bubble size. The keyhole fluctuation and bubble evolution mechanisms revealed here may guide the development of control systems for minimising porosity. Understanding the keyhole porosity formation is important in laser powder bed fusion. Here the authors reveal the dynamics of keyhole fluctuation, and collapse that induces bubble formation with three main stages of evolution; growth, shrinkage, and being captured by the solidification front.

{"answer": "## Measured Laser Absorptance of Aluminium Alloys at 1.03–1.08 µm in Conduction Mode and the Pre-Keyhole Transition

### 1. Overview

The question of what fraction of incident 1.07 µm laser power is actually coupled into an aluminium melt before a keyhole forms is central to any physics-based model of laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) of Al-Si alloys. The Drude–Fresnel absorptance of clean, smooth liquid aluminium at normal incidence near 1.07 µm is approximately 0.10–0.15, depending on the assumed electrical resistivity (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000003). In practice, every published measurement on a real surface under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode reports a value that significantly exceeds this clean-liquid prediction. The principal studies are summarised below and in the accompanying table.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 2. Trapp et al. (2017) — Al 1100 Bare Plate, Calorimetry

Trapp et al. used direct micro-calorimetry with a 1070 nm Yb-fibre laser focused to a 60 ± 5 µm (1/e²) Gaussian spot on 0.6 mm thick Al 1100 discs at scan speeds of 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). At 1500 mm/s, the conduction-mode absorptivity was approximately 0.10–0.15 and remained roughly constant across the low-power range (up to ≈200 W) where no melting or only shallow melting occurred. The onset of keyhole formation was observed at 265 ± 15 W at 1500 mm/s (Table 2 and Fig. 7 of that paper), after which absorptivity climbed steeply (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The extrapolated zero-power absorptivity for Al 1100 was notably higher than the clean-metal Fresnel prediction; Trapp et al. attributed this to enhanced absorption from the native aluminium oxide layer, noting that the discs were ground before experiments but not sputtered clean (pqac-00000010). For 316L steel at the same conditions, the flat-surface regime gave ≈ 0.29–0.31 for comparison (pqac-00000009). With a ≈100 µm powder layer on the Al 1100 substrate, absorptivity at low power was approximately twice that of the bare disc, then dropped sharply as powder melted, and rose again at keyhole onset (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011). DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006; key data in Fig. 7 and Table 2.

---

Laser Appl. 30, 032302, 2018; DOI: 10.2351/1.5040636) presented a companion publication from the same Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) calorimetric apparatus described by Trapp et al. state.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. Question: what laser absorptance has been MEASURED (integrating sphere or calorimetry) at 1.03-1.08 um for aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, Al 6061, Al 5182, Al 1100, pure Al) under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode and in the transition just before a keyhole forms, on bare plates and on powder layers? Include Simonds et al. 2024 (AM-Bench 2022, Al 5182), Trapp et al. 2017, Matthews et al. 2018 (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302), and any AlSi10Mg single-track absorptance. ---

### 2. Trapp et al. (2017) — Al 1100 Bare Plate, Calorimetry

Trapp et al. used direct micro-calorimetry with a 1070 nm Yb-fibre laser focused to a 60 ± 5 µm (1/e²) Gaussian spot on 0.6 mm thick Al 1100 discs at scan speeds of 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 2-3, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4). At 1500 mm/s, the conduction-mode absorptivity was approximately 0.10–0.15 and remained roughly constant across the low-power range (up to ≈200 W) where no melting or only shallow melting occurred. The onset of keyhole formation was observed at 265 ± 15 W at 1500 mm/s (Table 2 and Fig. 7 of that paper), after which absorptivity climbed steeply (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7). The extrapolated zero-power absorptivity for Al 1100 was notably higher than the clean-metal Fresnel prediction; Trapp et al. attributed this to enhanced absorption from the native aluminium oxide layer, noting that the discs were ground before experiments but not sputtered clean (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7). For 316L steel at the same conditions, the flat-surface regime gave ≈ 0.29–0.31 for comparison (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6). With a ≈100 µm powder layer on the Al 1100 substrate, absorptivity at low power was approximately twice that of the bare disc, then dropped sharply as powder melted, and rose again at keyhole onset (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 1-2, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006; key data in Fig. 7 and Table 2.

---

### 3. Matthews et al. (2018) — Al 1100, Calorimetry (Companion Paper)

Matthews, Trapp, Guss, and Rubenchik (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302, 2018; DOI: 10.2351/1.5040636) presented a companion publication from the same Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) calorimetric apparatus described by Trapp et al. (2017), reporting the same 1070 nm, 60 µm spot measurements on Al 1100 and 316L at 100–1500 mm/s (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 1-2). The full text of this paper could not be retrieved independently during this search, but its experimental parameters, materials, and results overlap with the Trapp 2017 dataset described above. The conduction-mode absorptivity of bare Al 1100 at 1500 mm/s remains ≈ 0.10–0.15 up to the keyhole transition.

---

### 4. Simonds et al. (2024) — Al 5182, Integrating-Sphere Radiometry (AM-Bench 2022)

Simonds et al. combined integrating-sphere radiometry (40 ns time resolution) with high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging at the Advanced Photon Source on 1 mm thick, mirror-polished bare plates of Al 5182 (NIST SRM 1241c) with a 1070 nm laser and a 122.5 µm (1/e²) spot diameter (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 1-3, simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 3-6).

**Stationary exposure (501 W, 1.982 ms):** The measured average absorptance before keyhole formation was ≈ 0.24 (≈ 24%), with the keyhole transition occurring at ≈ 0.189 ms, defined as the point where absorptance reached 0.35 (Figs. 2–4). After the keyhole formed, the average absorptance climbed to ≈ 0.65 (Fig. 4b) (simonds2024abilitytosimulate media 71f44c40, simonds2024abilitytosimulate media 99642dbd).

**Scanned exposure (473 W, 700 mm/s, 1.980 ms):** The pre-keyhole average absorptance was again ≈ 0.24, while the post-keyhole average was ≈ 0.44 (Figs. 6–8) (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 6-8, simonds2024abilitytosimulate media bd134611). Notably, the pre-keyhole absorptance of 0.24 significantly exceeds the clean Fresnel prediction for liquid aluminium (≈ 0.10–0.15). Simonds et al. concluded that "most simulations rely on literature values for optical properties... that are not representative of the aluminum material tested" and that "reflection and absorption are very sensitive to surface preparation" (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 6-8). They specifically highlighted that once a keyhole forms, the dependence on intrinsic optical properties largely disappears because multiple reflections dominate (simonds2024abilitytosimulate pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1007/s40192-023-00336-0; Figs. 4a and 8a.

---

### 5. Allen (2023 thesis, Chapter 5) & Reed (2024 thesis) — AlSi10Mg, ISR in a Commercial AM Machine

Allen et al. installed a custom integrating sphere directly inside a Renishaw AM 400 system and measured time-resolved absorptance at 260 kHz during multi-track LPBF of AlSi10Mg with plasma-atomised powder (D50 = 28 µm, 15–63 µm range) (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 115-120, allen2023sheddinglighton pages 124-129). This is the only known study reporting calibrated, time-resolved absorptance for AlSi10Mg powder layers under realistic AM conditions.

**Conduction mode (157 W, 70 µm spot, 60 µs exposure, ≈ 790 mm/s effective speed):**
- Machined bare AlSi10Mg substrate: 0.06 ± 0.02 (chapter summary) or 0.04 ± 0.04 (single illustrative trace) — the lowest value, consistent with a smooth, specularly reflecting metallic surface (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 138-143).
- AM-built substrate with no loose powder (AM0, rough hatched surface): 0.22 ± 0.05 — substantially higher due to periodic roughness from prior hatch lines (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 138-143).
- 30 µm nominal powder layer (AM30, actual thickness >120 µm): 0.77 ± 0.08 — high due to multiple scattering among powder particles (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 138-143, reed2024timeresolvedabsorptanceina pages 83-89).
- 90 µm nominal powder layer (AM90, actual thickness >180 µm): 0.74 ± 0.07 (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 138-143, reed2024timeresolvedabsorptanceina pages 83-89).

These are shown in Fig. 5.4 and summarised in Fig. 5.6 of the Allen thesis.

**Transition mode (375 W, 105 µm spot, 100 µs exposure, ≈ 500 mm/s):**
- Machined bare: average 0.30 ± 0.05, with sporadic temporary keyhole openings superimposed on a base of ≈ 0.10 (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 143-148).
- AM0 (rough): average 0.49 ± 0.07, base between keyholes ≈ 0.30 (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 143-148).
- AM30 powder: average 0.84 ± 0.10 (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 143-148).
- AM90 powder: average 0.74 ± 0.09, with signs of powder depletion by denudation reducing absorptance of later tracks by up to 40% (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 143-148).

Shown in Fig. 5.5 and Fig. 5.6. The Reed (2024) thesis reports the identical dataset and confirms all numerical values (reed2024timeresolvedabsorptanceinb pages 83-89, reed2024timeresolvedabsorptanceina pages 83-89).

---

### 6. Allen (2023 thesis, Chapter 4) — Al 6061, ISR + ICI Spot Welding

Using a 1070 nm multimode fibre laser with a 238 µm (1/e²) spot, Allen measured absorptance during 10 ms stationary spot welds on sanded Al 6061 at 974 W (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 110-115, allen2023sheddinglighton pages 100-105). After keyhole formation, the average absorptance was 0.723 ± 0.001. Reliable pre-keyhole absorptance data could not be obtained because back-reflections from the initially flat, highly reflective aluminium surface escaped the integrating sphere for up to 2.51 ms, before a keyhole tilted the reflected beam into the sphere walls (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 100-105). Published in Procedia CIRP 111, 5–9 (2022); DOI: 10.1016/j.procir.2022.08.041; data in Fig. 4.1 and summary Table 4.1.

---

### 7. Why Is the Measured Pre-Keyhole Absorptance Higher Than the Clean-Liquid Fresnel Value?

The user's model gives 0.18–0.20 from Drude–Fresnel optics of liquid Al-Si, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses ≈ 0.31. The experimental data above consistently report values between 0.06 and 0.24 on bare plates, depending on alloy and surface condition, with the difference from the idealized Fresnel prediction attributed to several factors:

**(a) Surface oxide.** Rubenchik et al. (2014) showed, through thin-film optical modelling at 780 nm, that a native alumina layer of only ≈ 50 nm thickness raises the absorptivity of engineering-grade aluminium from the clean-Fresnel value of ≈ 0.13 to above 0.20 (rubenchik2014temperaturedependent780nmlaser pages 4-5). The alumina refractive index (n ≈ 1.62 at 0.78 µm) modifies the boundary conditions for the incident light, acting as an anti-reflection coating; the effect carries over qualitatively to 1.07 µm. Trapp et al. noted that the extrapolated zero-power absorptivity of Al 1100 exceeded the literature value for clean metal and attributed this to oxide, "even though this effect is considered to be small as the discs were ground before the experiments" (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7).

**(b) Surface roughness/corrugation.** Rubenchik et al. (2014) further demonstrated, using polarisation-resolved measurements, that surface corrugation couples incident radiation into surface electromagnetic modes (surface plasmons), producing absorptance in excess of what oxide alone can explain (rubenchik2014temperaturedependent780nmlaser pages 4-5). In the Allen AlSi10Mg data, the hatched AM0 substrate (periodic roughness from prior hatch lines at 35 µm spacing) absorbed 0.22, nearly four times the machined substrate value of 0.06 (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 138-143), providing direct evidence that micron-scale roughness dramatically increases coupling in conduction mode.

**(c) Shallow vapour depression (pre-keyhole).** At the transition, before a true keyhole with an aspect ratio > 1 is established, Trapp et al. observed (at 68 W, 500 mm/s on 316L) the intermittent appearance of a small depression (≈ 30 µm deep) lasting only ≈ 50 µs before collapsing, with associated fluctuations in absorptance (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6). Allen et al. observed analogous temporary depressions in AlSi10Mg causing sporadic absorptance spikes from 0.10 to > 0.50 on bare machined surfaces at 375 W (allen2023sheddinglighton pages 143-148). These shallow depressions allow one or two additional Fresnel reflections (the coupling expected for a cone of aspect ratio ≈ 1 is ≈ 0.58), and their time-averaged contribution raises the apparent absorptance above the flat-surface value.

**(d) Vapour/plume absorption.** Trapp et al. discussed the possibility that laser light may be absorbed or reflected in the vapour plume before reaching the metallic surface, noting that the plume tilts more with increasing scan speed, reducing plume–beam interaction (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7). However, vapour-plume absorption is generally considered small relative to the oxide and roughness effects for aluminium at 1.07 µm in the conduction-mode regime.

**In summary:** The measured pre-keyhole absorptance of bare aluminium (0.10–0.24) exceeds the clean-liquid Drude–Fresnel prediction (0.10–0.15) primarily because of native oxide films and surface roughness/corrugation, with an additional contribution from intermittent shallow depressions at the transition. Vapour/plume absorption is a minor contributor. The Thermo-Calc AM Module's value of ≈ 0.31 likely reflects an engineering compromise that lumps oxide, roughness, and incipient depression effects into a single effective absorptance; it is higher than most bare-plate measurements but lower than any powder-covered measurement (≈ 0.65–0.77).

---

### 8. Summary of Key Figures and DOIs

- **Trapp et al. (2017):** Fig. 7 (Al 1100 vs 316L vs W absorptivity at 1500 mm/s), Table 2 (keyhole thresholds), Fig. 6 (powder vs bare 316L). DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006.
- **Matthews et al. (2018):** Companion to Trapp 2017. DOI: 10.2351/1.5040636.
- **Simonds et al. (2024):** Fig. 2 (stationary Al 5182 absorptance vs time), Fig. 4a (pre-keyhole experimental value ≈ 24%), Fig. 8a (scanned pre-keyhole ≈ 24%). DOI: 10.1007/s40192-023-00336-0.
- **Allen (2023 thesis, Ch. 5):** Fig. 5.4 (time-resolved absorptance for AlSi10Mg, four surface conditions), Fig. 5.6 (all average absorptance vs power).
- **Reed (2024 thesis):** Confirms Allen values; conduction and transition time-trace figures in results chapter.
- **Allen et al. / Allen thesis Ch. 4 (Al 6061):** Fig. 4.1, Table 4.1 (keyhole absorptance 0.72). DOI: 10.1016/j.procir.2022.08.041.
- **Rubenchik et al. (2014):** Oxide thin-film model and polarisation data for engineering-grade Al at 780 nm. DOI: 10.1117/1.OE.53.12.122506.

---

### 2. Trapp et al. (2017) — Al 1100 Bare Plate, Calorimetry

Trapp et al. used direct micro-calorimetry with a 1070 nm Yb-fibre laser focused to a 60 ± 5 µm (1/e²) Gaussian spot on 0.6 mm thick Al 1100 discs at scan speeds of 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). At 1500 mm/s, the conduction-mode absorptivity was approximately 0.10–0.15 and remained roughly constant across the low-power range (up to ≈200 W) where no melting or only shallow melting occurred. The onset of keyhole formation was observed at 265 ± 15 W at 1500 mm/s (Table 2 and Fig. 7 of that paper), after which absorptivity climbed steeply (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The extrapolated zero-power absorptivity for Al 1100 was notably higher than the clean-metal Fresnel prediction; Trapp et al. attributed this to enhanced absorption from the native aluminium oxide layer, noting that the discs were ground before experiments but not sputtered clean (pqac-00000010). For 316L steel at the same conditions, the flat-surface regime gave ≈ 0.29–0.31 for comparison (pqac-00000009). With a ≈100 µm powder layer on the Al 1100 substrate, absorptivity at low power was approximately twice that of the bare disc, then dropped sharply as powder melted, and rose again at keyhole onset (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011). DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006; key data in Fig. 7 and Table 2.

---

### 3. Matthews et al. (2018) — Al 1100, Calorimetry (Companion Paper)

Matthews, Trapp, Guss, and Rubenchik (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302, 2018; DOI: 10.2351/1.5040636) presented a companion publication from the same Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) calorimetric apparatus described by Trapp et al. (2017), reporting the same 1070 nm, 60 µm spot measurements on Al 1100 and 316L at 100–1500 mm/s (pqac-00000045). The full text of this paper could not be retrieved independently during this search, but its experimental parameters, materials, and results overlap with the Trapp 2017 dataset described above. The conduction-mode absorptivity of bare Al 1100 at 1500 mm/s remains ≈ 0.10–0.15 up to the keyhole transition.

---

### 4. Simonds et al. (2024) — Al 5182, Integrating-Sphere Radiometry (AM-Bench 2022)

Simonds et al. combined integrating-sphere radiometry (40 ns time resolution) with high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging at the Advanced Photon Source on 1 mm thick, mirror-polished bare plates of Al 5182 (NIST SRM 1241c) with a 1070 nm laser and a 122.5 µm (1/e²) spot diameter (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Stationary exposure (501 W, 1.982 ms):** The measured average absorptance before keyhole formation was ≈ 0.24 (≈ 24%), with the keyhole transition occurring at ≈ 0.189 ms, defined as the point where absorptance reached 0.35 (Figs. 2–4). After the keyhole formed, the average absorptance climbed to ≈ 0.65 (Fig. 4b) (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000043).

**Scanned exposure (473 W, 700 mm/s, 1.980 ms):** The pre-keyhole average absorptance was again ≈ 0.24, while the post-keyhole average was ≈ 0.44 (Figs. 6–8) (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000044). Notably, the pre-keyhole absorptance of 0.24 significantly exceeds the clean Fresnel prediction for liquid aluminium (≈ 0.10–0.15). Simonds et al. concluded that "most simulations rely on literature values for optical properties... that are not representative of the aluminum material tested" and that "reflection and absorption are very sensitive to surface preparation" (pqac-00000014). They specifically highlighted that once a keyhole forms, the dependence on intrinsic optical properties largely disappears because multiple reflections dominate (pqac-00000013). DOI: 10.1007/s40192-023-00336-0; Figs. 4a and 8a.

---

### 5. Allen (2023 thesis, Chapter 5) & Reed (2024 thesis) — AlSi10Mg, ISR in a Commercial AM Machine

Allen et al. installed a custom integrating sphere directly inside a Renishaw AM 400 system and measured time-resolved absorptance at 260 kHz during multi-track LPBF of AlSi10Mg with plasma-atomised powder (D50 = 28 µm, 15–63 µm range) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). This is the only known study reporting calibrated, time-resolved absorptance for AlSi10Mg powder layers under realistic AM conditions.

**Conduction mode (157 W, 70 µm spot, 60 µs exposure, ≈ 790 mm/s effective speed):**
- Machined bare AlSi10Mg substrate: 0.06 ± 0.02 (chapter summary) or 0.04 ± 0.04 (single illustrative trace) — the lowest value, consistent with a smooth, specularly reflecting metallic surface (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000029).
- AM-built substrate with no loose powder (AM0, rough hatched surface): 0.22 ± 0.05 — substantially higher due to periodic roughness from prior hatch lines (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000029).
- 30 µm nominal powder layer (AM30, actual thickness >120 µm): 0.77 ± 0.08 — high due to multiple scattering among powder particles (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000025).
- 90 µm nominal powder layer (AM90, actual thickness >180 µm): 0.74 ± 0.07 (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000025).

These are shown in Fig. 5.4 and summarised in Fig. 5.6 of the Allen thesis.

**Transition mode (375 W, 105 µm spot, 100 µs exposure, ≈ 500 mm/s):**
- Machined bare: average 0.30 ± 0.05, with sporadic temporary keyhole openings superimposed on a base of ≈ 0.10 (pqac-00000042).
- AM0 (rough): average 0.49 ± 0.07, base between keyholes ≈ 0.30 (pqac-00000042).
- AM30 powder: average 0.84 ± 0.10 (pqac-00000042).
- AM90 powder: average 0.74 ± 0.09, with signs of powder depletion by denudation reducing absorptance of later tracks by up to 40% (pqac-00000042).

Shown in Fig. 5.5 and Fig. 5.6. The Reed (2024) thesis reports the identical dataset and confirms all numerical values (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001).

---

### 6. Allen (2023 thesis, Chapter 4) — Al 6061, ISR + ICI Spot Welding

Using a 1070 nm multimode fibre laser with a 238 µm (1/e²) spot, Allen measured absorptance during 10 ms stationary spot welds on sanded Al 6061 at 974 W (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000022). After keyhole formation, the average absorptance was 0.723 ± 0.001. Reliable pre-keyhole absorptance data could not be obtained because back-reflections from the initially flat, highly reflective aluminium surface escaped the integrating sphere for up to 2.51 ms, before a keyhole tilted the reflected beam into the sphere walls (pqac-00000022). Published in Procedia CIRP 111, 5–9 (2022); DOI: 10.1016/j.procir.2022.08.041; data in Fig. 4.1 and summary Table 4.1.

---

### 7. Why Is the Measured Pre-Keyhole Absorptance Higher Than the Clean-Liquid Fresnel Value?

The user's model gives 0.18–0.20 from Drude–Fresnel optics of liquid Al-Si, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses ≈ 0.31. The experimental data above consistently report values between 0.06 and 0.24 on bare plates, depending on alloy and surface condition, with the difference from the idealized Fresnel prediction attributed to several factors:

**(a) Surface oxide.** Rubenchik et al. (2014) showed, through thin-film optical modelling at 780 nm, that a native alumina layer of only ≈ 50 nm thickness raises the absorptivity of engineering-grade aluminium from the clean-Fresnel value of ≈ 0.13 to above 0.20 (pqac-00000052). The alumina refractive index (n ≈ 1.62 at 0.78 µm) modifies the boundary conditions for the incident light, acting as an anti-reflection coating; the effect carries over qualitatively to 1.07 µm. Trapp et al. noted that the extrapolated zero-power absorptivity of Al 1100 exceeded the literature value for clean metal and attributed this to oxide, "even though this effect is considered to be small as the discs were ground before the experiments" (pqac-00000010).

**(b) Surface roughness/corrugation.** Rubenchik et al. (2014) further demonstrated, using polarisation-resolved measurements, that surface corrugation couples incident radiation into surface electromagnetic modes (surface plasmons), producing absorptance in excess of what oxide alone can explain (pqac-00000052). In the Allen AlSi10Mg data, the hatched AM0 substrate (periodic roughness from prior hatch lines at 35 µm spacing) absorbed 0.22, nearly four times the machined substrate value of 0.06 (pqac-00000041), providing direct evidence that micron-scale roughness dramatically increases coupling in conduction mode.

**(c) Shallow vapour depression (pre-keyhole).** At the transition, before a true keyhole with an aspect ratio > 1 is established, Trapp et al. observed (at 68 W, 500 mm/s on 316L) the intermittent appearance of a small depression (≈ 30 µm deep) lasting only ≈ 50 µs before collapsing, with associated fluctuations in absorptance (pqac-00000009). Allen et al. observed analogous temporary depressions in AlSi10Mg causing sporadic absorptance spikes from 0.10 to > 0.50 on bare machined surfaces at 375 W (pqac-00000042). These shallow depressions allow one or two additional Fresnel reflections (the coupling expected for a cone of aspect ratio ≈ 1 is ≈ 0.58), and their time-averaged contribution raises the apparent absorptance above the flat-surface value.

**(d) Vapour/plume absorption.** Trapp et al. discussed the possibility that laser light may be absorbed or reflected in the vapour plume before reaching the metallic surface, noting that the plume tilts more with increasing scan speed, reducing plume–beam interaction (pqac-00000010). However, vapour-plume absorption is generally considered small relative to the oxide and roughness effects for aluminium at 1.07 µm in the conduction-mode regime.

**In summary:** The measured pre-keyhole absorptance of bare aluminium (0.10–0.24) exceeds the clean-liquid Drude–Fresnel prediction (0.10–0.15) primarily because of native oxide films and surface roughness/corrugation, with an additional contribution from intermittent shallow depressions at the transition. Vapour/plume absorption is a minor contributor. The Thermo-Calc AM Module's value of ≈ 0.31 likely reflects an engineering compromise that lumps oxide, roughness, and incipient depression effects into a single effective absorptance; it is higher than most bare-plate measurements but lower than any powder-covered measurement (≈ 0.65–0.77).

---

### 8. Summary of Key Figures and DOIs

- **Trapp et al. (2017):** Fig. 7 (Al 1100 vs 316L vs W absorptivity at 1500 mm/s), Table 2 (keyhole thresholds), Fig. 6 (powder vs bare 316L). DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006.
- **Matthews et al. (2018):** Companion to Trapp 2017. DOI: 10.2351/1.5040636.
- **Simonds et al. (2024):** Fig. 2 (stationary Al 5182 absorptance vs time), Fig. 4a (pre-keyhole experimental value ≈ 24%), Fig. 8a (scanned pre-keyhole ≈ 24%). DOI: 10.1007/s40192-023-00336-0.
- **Allen (2023 thesis, Ch. 5):** Fig. 5.4 (time-resolved absorptance for AlSi10Mg, four surface conditions), Fig. 5.6 (all average absorptance vs power).
- **Reed (2024 thesis):** Confirms Allen values; conduction and transition time-trace figures in results chapter.
- **Allen et al. / Allen thesis Ch. 4 (Al 6061):** Fig. 4.1, Table 4.1 (keyhole absorptance 0.72). DOI: 10.1016/j.procir.2022.08.041.
- **Rubenchik et al. (2014):** Oxide thin-film model and polarisation data for engineering-grade Al at 780 nm. DOI: 10.1117/1.OE.53.12.122506.

contexts.context: Trapp et al. (Applied Materials Today 9, 2017, pp. 341–349) report bare-disc laser scans: aluminum melting power 125 W and calculated boiling power 473/107 W (analytic/FEM); observed melting <30 W and boiling/keyhole onset 265 ± 15 W. Absorptivity changes little before keyholing, then rises steeply at the deep-penetration onset and saturates around 0.7–0.8 for steel. The increase is attributed to recoil-pressure depression and multiple reflections on keyhole walls; oxide can raise zero-power aluminum absorptivity. Vapor absorption limits saturation.
contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. At 0.35 MW/cm² (conduction), absorptance plateaued at 0.21 in argon but rose to 0.51 in air, attributed primarily to oxidation. At 0.46 MW/cm² (transition), temporary keyholes in air raised absorptance to 0.56 through multiple reflections; oscillations occurred otherwise. At 0.58 MW/cm² (keyhole), both gases rapidly formed sustained keyholes. Threshold coupling efficiencies were 0.58 (air) and 0.59 (argon), interpreted as a shallow cavity enabling roughly two reflections. DOI, alloy, wavelength, power, speed, spot size, and powder-layer data are not given.
contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. Question: what laser absorptance has been MEASURED (integrating sphere or calorimetry) at 1.03-1.08 um for aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, Al 6061, Al 5182, Al 1100, pure Al) under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode and in the transition just before a keyhole forms, on bare plates and on powder layers? Include Simonds et al. 2024 (AM-Bench 2022, Al 5182), Trapp et al. 2017, Matthews et al. 2018 (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302), and any AlSi10Mg single-track absorptance. Give the power, speed, spot size, the measured absorptance against time or power, and the DOI with the figure or table number. Is the higher value attributed to surface oxide, ripples, a shallow depression, or vapour?

Samples sit 5 mm inside the sphere, with an 11° laser incidence chosen to avoid direct back-reflection; powder suppresses specular reflection. A 1070 nm band-pass filter excludes blackbody radiation, and a photodiode records scattered laser intensity at 1 μs resolution (3.8 μs rise time). Laser power is calibrated using 1–2 s PRIMES Cube measurements, while time-dependent pulse trains are reconstructed from photodiode traces and normalized using a diffuse gold target.
contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. Question: what laser absorptance has been MEASURED (integrating sphere or calorimetry) at 1.03-1.08 um for aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, Al 6061, Al 5182, Al 1100, pure Al) under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode and in the transition just before a keyhole forms, on bare plates and on powder layers? Include Simonds et al. 2024 (AM-Bench 2022, Al 5182), Trapp et al. 2017, Matthews et al. 2018 (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302), and any AlSi10Mg single-track absorptance. Give the power, speed, spot size, the measured absorptance against time or power, and the DOI with the figure or table number. Is the higher value attributed to surface oxide, ripples, a shallow depression, or vapour?

contexts.context: Simonds et al.’s ISR measurements on AlSi10Mg used 375 W, 105-µm spot, 100-µs exposures over five adjacent 10-mm tracks (Fig. 5.5). Bare AM0 substrate averaged ~0.30 without keyholes and 0.49±0.07 with intermittent keyholes; machined plate averaged 0.10 and 0.30±0.05. Powder layers were much higher: 30-µm powder, 0.84±0.10; 90-µm, 0.74±0.09. At ≤247 W, AM powder measured 0.65–0.76, AM0 0.16–0.23, machined 0.02–0.09 (Fig. 5.6). Keyholing began near 270–325 W, producing sustained absorptance >0.5; powder behavior was attributed mainly to geometry, denudation, and changing surface area.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes how increasing laser power or dwell time drives melting from conduction through transition to keyhole mode as melt-pool/vapor-depression aspect ratio increases. Vaporization creates a deep, narrow cavity with downward multiple reflections, maximal temperatures at its bottom, and upward vapor ejection. It emphasizes that keyhole walls develop protrusions and unstable vapor-driven flows, producing fast spatters (>40 m/s cited for Ti-6Al-4V) and pores. However, it provides no quantitative laser absorptance measurements, material-specific Al data, laser parameters, DOI, or figure/table values for Al alloys.
contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. Question: what laser absorptance has been MEASURED (integrating sphere or calorimetry) at 1.03-1.08 um for aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, Al 6061, Al 5182, Al 1100, pure Al) under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode and in the transition just before a keyhole forms, on bare plates and on powder layers? Include Simonds et al. 2024 (AM-Bench 2022, Al 5182), Trapp et al. 2017, Matthews et al. 2018 (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302), and any AlSi10Mg single-track absorptance. Give the power, speed, spot size, the measured absorptance against time or power, and the DOI with the figure or table number. Is the higher value attributed to surface oxide, ripples, a shallow depression, or vapour?

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns molten aluminum oxide (Al2O3), not liquid metallic aluminum, and therefore does not directly establish why aluminum’s absorptance exceeds a clean-liquid-metal Fresnel prediction or distinguish among surface oxide, roughness/ripples, vapor depression, and plume absorption. It does, however, provide evidence that the surrounding chemical environment strongly affects molten alumina absorption. In experiments on a sapphire fiber, the absorption coefficient was reported to be 4–6 times higher in oxygen than in argon; an atmosphere containing 10% H2 and 90% N2 produced a value about 1.5 times higher than argon. The absorption changed after melting and stabilized over time, with stabilization taking approximately 30 minutes after switching from argon to oxygen. The authors state that the long-wavelength edge of electronic absorption shifted toward longer wavelengths in oxygen. These observations support a role for oxygen-related chemical modification—potentially oxide formation or altered melt composition/electronic absorption—but they do not quantify the role of an oxide layer on aluminum at 1070 nm. No evidence in this excerpt addresses surface roughness, ripples, shallow vapor depressions, or absorption by a vapor/plume above liquid aluminum.

Is the higher absorptance attributed to surface oxide, surface roughness/ripples, a shallow vapor depression, or vapour/plume absorption? contexts.context: The excerpt supports surface oxidation as the principal explanation for aluminum absorptance exceeding the clean-surface optical prediction. In the aluminum experiments, absorptance increased after repeated heating and cooling cycles, and the authors identify modification of the oxide layer as evidence for that increase. Their thin-film calculation indicates that increasing the aluminum oxide thickness from approximately 50 to 70 nm could account for the measured change. Surface roughness changes and defect generation are also mentioned as possible contributing factors, but they are presented as secondary or additional possibilities rather than the primary explanation. contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically identify which mechanism explains aluminum’s absorptance exceeding a clean-liquid-metal Fresnel prediction, and it does not discuss oxide quantitatively at 1070 nm. It does, however, emphasize that Fresnel-type reflectivity predictions apply to idealized surfaces, whereas laser-heated surfaces can undergo melting, decomposition, ablation, and changes in composition and quality. Surface roughness lowers reflectivity and increases absorption because the laser can undergo multiple reflections between surface peaks and valleys; the reflected light also becomes more diffuse and less specular. Consequently, roughness or laser-induced ripples could make measured absorptance exceed the value predicted for a smooth, clean liquid surface. The passage also notes that reflectivity decreases sharply as the metal heats toward melting, partly because electrical conductivity falls, and that alternative interpretations of transient reflectance changes include surface deformation and plasma absorption or scattering. These points support considering surface morphology, temperature-dependent optical properties, and plume/plasma effects when interpreting measurements. The provided pages contain no direct evidence establishing whether a surface oxide, shallow vapor depression, or vapor/plume absorption is dominant, nor do they state the specific role of oxide at 1070 nm.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that the higher measured absorptance of engineering-grade aluminum, compared with ideal clean or vacuum-deposited metal predictions, is generally attributed to the real surface rather than to the intrinsic Fresnel response of pure metal. Specifically, it identifies surface roughness, oxide films, and absorbing impurities as likely causes. The excerpt does not provide evidence that a shallow vapor depression, surface ripples, or absorption by a vapor/plume is responsible, nor does it separate quantitatively the contributions of roughness and oxide. It also notes that absorptance can increase with temperature because increased electron–phonon collisions raise free-electron absorption, although this is a temperature effect rather than necessarily an explanation for the room-temperature discrepancy. For oxide, the text states that aluminum is coated by an oxide layer that is transparent through the UV range and has a relatively high refractive index (n = 1.62 at 0.78 μm). Thus, the oxide can alter the optical boundary conditions and measured absorptance despite being nominally transparent. However, this excerpt does not specifically quantify the oxide contribution at 1070 nm or establish whether it increases or decreases absorptance there; that conclusion would require the subsequent discussion or data from the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares measured aluminum absorptivity with the low Fresnel prediction for bulk, clean aluminum at 780 nm: the calculated absorptivity is approximately 0.13. An oxide coating can substantially increase absorption; the article’s thin-film calculation indicates that an oxide layer of about 50 nm can produce absorptivity above 20%, with thickness variability producing correspondingly different values. However, the authors explicitly state that oxide increases absorptivity but is not sufficient by itself to explain the measured results. They attribute the additional absorption primarily to surface roughness or corrugation, which enhances coupling of incident radiation into surface electromagnetic waves (plasmons). The polarization experiment supports this interpretation: light with its electric field orthogonal to the grooves has higher absorption because it is p-polarized relative to the corrugated surface, whereas the parallel orientation is s-polarized. The excerpt does not discuss a shallow vapor depression, plume/vapor absorption, or measurements specifically at 1070 nm. Thus, based on this passage, oxide is an important contributor but not the complete explanation; roughness/corrugation is identified as the dominant additional mechanism.

Question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Our model's melt absorbs only 0.18-0.20 (Fresnel, clean liquid Al-Si) in the regime where the surface boils but no keyhole has formed, while the Thermo-Calc AM Module uses about 0.31 there. Question: what laser absorptance has been MEASURED (integrating sphere or calorimetry) at 1.03-1.08 um for aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, Al 6061, Al 5182, Al 1100, pure Al) under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode and in the transition just before a keyhole forms, on bare plates and on powder layers? Include Simonds et al. 2024 (AM-Bench 2022, Al 5182), Trapp et al. 2017, Matthews et al. 2018 (J. Laser Appl. 30, 032302), and any AlSi10Mg single-track absorptance. Give the power, speed, spot size, the measured absorptance against time or power, and the DOI with the figure or table number. Is the higher value attributed to surface oxide, ripples, a shallow depression, or vapour?

## Measured Laser Absorptance of Aluminium Alloys at 1.03–1.08 µm in Conduction Mode and the Pre-Keyhole Transition

### 1. Overview

The question of what fraction of incident 1.07 µm laser power is actually coupled into an aluminium melt before a keyhole forms is central to any physics-based model of laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) of Al-Si alloys. The Drude–Fresnel absorptance of clean, smooth liquid aluminium at normal incidence near 1.07 µm is approximately 0.10–0.15, depending on the assumed electrical resistivity (reed2024timeresolvedabsorptancein pages 27-31, reed2024timeresolvedabsorptanceina pages 27-31). In practice, every published measurement on a real surface under a moving or stationary laser in conduction mode reports a value that significantly exceeds this clean-liquid prediction. The principal studies are summarised below and in the accompanying table.
